q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT (c1)) >= 2
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear different because one writes GROUP BY c4, c3 with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 and orders by ID while the other writes GROUP BY c3, c4 with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) >= 2. However, note that (a) grouping by (c4, c3) is the same as grouping by (c3, c4) (the order of grouping columns does not change the grouping), (b) the condition 'COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1' is equivalent to 'COUNT(DISTINCT c1) >= 2' since count returns an integer, and (c) the SELECT DISTINCT c3 simply returns the set of c3 values coming from groups that meet the condition. In standard SQL, these two queries are semantically equivalent. In other words, for any dataset the two queries would yield the same set of IDs (even though one query specifies an ORDER BY which only affects presentation, not the set of rows).
counterexample_dsp: Because the only differences are a reordering of GROUP BY columns and a rewritten (but equivalent) HAVING condition, no true counterexample exists where the two queries output different results. (One may try to force a difference by appealing to result ordering, but since SQL result sets are unordered by definition, the two queries are equivalent in essence.)

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT SUM(c5) AS c5 FROM table1 AS A WHERE 1 <= ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1 WHERE A.c3 != c3 AND c4 = A.c4 ) AND (A.c1, A.c2) NOT IN ( SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 WHERE A.c3 != c3 )
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to sum c5 values for rows that have a duplicate c4 value and a unique (c1, c2) value. Q1 does this by grouping non‐correlated subqueries (one to pick c4 that occurs more than once and one to pick unique (c1, c2) groups), while Q2 uses correlated subqueries. In particular, Q2’s second condition uses a NOT IN over a subquery that returns every (c1,c2) from other rows. If any of those rows has a NULL in one component then the NOT IN predicate will evaluate to UNKNOWN (and so exclude a row) even if the candidate row’s (c1,c2) is unique. In our counterexample the candidate rows would be accepted by Q1 (since their groupings yield count = 1) but rejected by Q2 because the subquery for one row contains a row with a NULL value.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 10, 100, 1, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c5, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 10, 200, NULL, 2);
counterexample_dsp: We construct two rows with the same c4 so that the c4 duplicated condition holds. Each row’s (c1,c2) is unique when grouped. However, one row has a NULL for c1. In Q1 the grouping sees (1,1) and (NULL,2) as unique groups and includes both rows; Q2’s correlated subquery, when run on either row, returns a tuple containing a NULL (either from the row with NULL c1 or from the other row), and the NOT IN predicate then fails (since unknown comparisons in a NOT IN list cause the condition to evaluate as false). Thus, Q1 sums c5 from both rows, while Q2 sums nothing.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they treat a group produced by table2 that does not have a matching row in table1. Q1 is built using an inner join between table1 and a sub‐query (which groups table2 by c3 using date conditions) so it returns only those c3 values for which table1 has a row. In contrast, Q2 builds a CTE (using the same grouping on table2) and then left‐joins table1. That means that if a c3 appears in table2 and satisfies the date conditions but there is no corresponding row in table1, Q2 will still return that c3 (with a NULL for P.c4), whereas Q1 will omit it. (Note that according to the declared foreign key every table2.c3 should have a matching table1 row. However, if for example the foreign key were deferrable or temporarily disabled, one can construct a counterexample in which table2 contains a “orphan” grouping.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert one valid row in table1 (with c3 = 1) and a corresponding row in table2 for c3 = 1 that meets the date criteria. Also insert into table2 an extra row for c3 = 2 with a date within the allowed range but do not insert a matching row into table1. Then Q1 (using an inner join) will return only the row for c3 = 1, while Q2 (using a left join) will return two rows – one for c3 = 1 and an extra row for c3 = 2 with a NULL in c4. (The extra row in table2 is “orphaned” from table1; note that in many systems the foreign key would prevent such an insert, but for the purpose of the counterexample we assume that the FK is either deferrable or disabled during data load.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT V.c2 AS ID FROM table1 AS V JOIN table1 ON V.c2 = V.c3 ORDER BY ID
explanation: Q1 returns only the rows from table1 where c2 equals c3 (so it picks values whose appearance is self‐matched), whereas Q2 – as intended – is written to join table1 (aliased as V) with table1 using a join condition that was meant to compare V.c2 with the other table’s c3. In that intended version, Q2 returns every V.c2 for which there exists some row in table1 whose c3 equals V.c2. As a result, a row that does not satisfy V.c2 = V.c3 (and so is not produced by Q1) may still appear in Q2 if its c2 occurs as some row’s c3. This difference in the “filtering” (a per‐row self match in Q1 versus an existence check via the join in Q2) causes the two queries to produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: We can demonstrate the difference by inserting three rows. One row (for example, with c2=3 and c3=3) qualifies for Q1 because c2 and c3 match in that same row. The other two rows have c2 != c3, so Q1 will ignore them. However, if we choose the values appropriately – for instance, one row with c2=1 and c3=2 and another row with c2=2 and c3=1 – then each of these nonqualifying rows has a c2 value that appears as c3 in another row. Thus, when using the join condition (interpreted as V.c2 = table1.c3), both of these rows produce join pairs and their c2 values appear in Q2. Therefore, Q1 returns only {3} while Q2 returns {1,2,3}. Note that the schema imposes no NOT NULL, PK, or UNIQUE constraints so these simple integers and dates are fine.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 filter rows where c1 is between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27', group by c1 (using the column itself in Q1 and the column position in Q2), and then compute COUNT(DISTINCT c4) over each group. The extra HAVING clause in Q2 (HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1) is redundant because a GROUP BY always produces groups with at least one row. As a result, for any valid data that respects the schema and constraints, Q1 and Q2 will always produce identical outputs.
counterexample_dsp: There is no possible test dataset that can trigger a behavioral difference between these two queries. Any dataset (including edge cases with duplicate or NULL values in c4, or multiple rows per day) will yield the same aggregation results in Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(c1 - RNK) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT c1, LAG(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c1) AS RNK FROM table1) AS T
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the minimum distance between two distinct numbers in table1. Q1 does so by taking every unordered pair (A, B) with A.c1 <> B.c1 and computing MIN(ABS(A.c1 - B.c1)), whereas Q2 orders the rows by c1 and then computes the gap c1 - LAG(c1) (i.e. the difference only between consecutive numbers) and returns its minimum. For any non‐empty table that holds at least two distinct numbers, it is a well–known fact that the least absolute difference is achieved by two consecutive numbers when they are sorted. However, consider the “edge case” when the table does not contain two rows. If there is only one row then the join in Q1 produces no pairs—so in many SQL implementations the aggregate MIN over an empty set yields a single row with a NULL value (or sometimes no row at all), while Q2 always produces one row (its single row’s LAG value is NULL so the expression c1 - RNK is NULL, and MIN over a single NULL gives NULL). Depending on the SQL dialect the difference in result “shape” (no row versus a row with NULL) is observable. This shows that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent when table1 contains fewer than two rows.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row into table1. Under some SQL implementations, Q1 (which joins table1 with itself and then applies the condition A.c1 <> B.c1) produces an empty set (or an aggregate over an empty set, which may not yield a row), while Q2 always returns exactly one row (with a NULL in SHORTEST). This difference in the number of output rows (or in how the empty aggregate is represented) is a counterexample.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,

);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RI FROM table1) AS A WHERE RI = 1
explanation: Q1 groups table1 by c4 and finds the minimum c2 for each group, then returns every row whose (c4, c2) pair matches one of these (c4, MIN(c2)) tuples. Q2 partitions the data by c4 and orders each partition by c2, then returns only the single row with the smallest c2 in each partition (using ROW_NUMBER() = 1). In a situation where multiple rows in a given c4 group share the same minimum c2 value, Q1 would return all those rows while Q2 would return an arbitrary one among them. However, because the schema defines a primary key on (c4, c2), no two rows can have the same values for c4 and c2. This inherent uniqueness guarantees that within each group the minimum c2 is unique, so the two queries will always return the same result.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would require a case where, for some c4 value, there are at least two rows having the same (minimum) c2 but different c1 values, which would cause Q1 to return both rows while Q2 returns only one. Due to the primary key constraint (c4, c2), such a scenario is impossible under the current schema.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT A.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT B.c1 FROM table2 B WHERE B.c1 = A.c2)
explanation: The two queries differ because of how NULLs are handled by the NOT IN versus the NOT EXISTS subquery. In Q1, if the subquery returns any NULL value, then the comparison c2 NOT IN (subquery) becomes UNKNOWN (and thus false) for every row. By contrast, Q2’s NOT EXISTS is not affected by the presence of NULL values since it only checks for matching rows, so a row in table1 with no matching non‐NULL value in table2 will still be returned.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'row1');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table1 (with c2 = 1) and one row into table2 with a NULL in column c1. Because table2 has a row with NULL, the NOT IN subquery in Q1 evaluates to false for the row in table1, causing Q1 to return no results, while Q2 returns that row. This highlights how Q1 and Q2 can behave differently due to the NULL in the subquery.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: At first glance both queries join table2 with table1 on c1 and then compute a rounded average of table1.c2 grouped by a column named c4. In Q1 the GROUP BY explicitly uses A.c4 (i.e. table2.c4), while in Q2 the GROUP BY uses an unqualified c4. Under the given schema (where only table2 has a column named c4) both queries are equivalent. However, if one were to extend the schema so that table1 also had a column named c4 (which is allowed in many databases even though it isn’t used as a key), then the two queries could behave differently. In that case Q1 would still group by table2.c4 while Q2, because its GROUP BY clause lists an unqualified c4, might be resolved by the SQL engine to mean table1.c4 (for example, if the SQL engine resolves unqualified names by scanning the FROM‐list in order). This potential ambiguity would then yield different grouping and hence different average results.
counterexample_dsp: Assume an extended schema where table1 has an extra integer column named c4. Then if we insert one row in table1 with c1 = 1 carrying c4 = 999 and a matching row in table2 with (c4 = 100, c1 = 1), Q1 will report group 100 (from table2) while Q2 – if its unqualified reference to c4 resolves to the table1 column – will group by 999. Thus, the two queries yield different results. (Note: Under the originally given schema no counterexample exists because table1 does not have a column c4. This example relies on a schema change that introduces a naming ambiguity in Q2.)

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT T.c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS CPC FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS T, (SELECT COUNT(c2) AS PC FROM table2) AS T2 WHERE PC = CPC
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because both compare a count computed over table1 (grouped by c1) with a count computed over table2. In Q1 the count on table2 is computed as COUNT(DISTINCT c2) while in Q2 it is computed as COUNT(c2). Under the given schema the column table2.c2 is the primary key – and table1.c1 is also a primary key – so (a) table2 never contains duplicate or NULL values and (b) each group in table1 has exactly one row. Therefore, for any valid data the value of COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is identical to COUNT(c2) and the aggregate on table1 is either 1 (for a non‐NULL c2) or 0 (if c2 is NULL). In such cases the two queries always return the same result. (In contrast, if the schema did not require c2 to be unique in table2 or allowed multiple rows per grouping in table1 then the use of DISTINCT in one part but not the other could yield differences.)
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample that makes Q1 and Q2 differ would require data that forces the two different ways of counting table2 to diverge – for example, by having duplicate non‐NULL values in table2 (so that COUNT(c2) is larger than COUNT(DISTINCT c2)) or by having multiple rows per group in table1 (so that a group’s COUNT(DISTINCT c2) can be > 1). However, the declared primary key constraints on table2 (on c2) and on table1 (on c1) rule out these possibilities. (It is only in a relaxed schema – where duplicates are allowed – that a counterexample can be constructed.)

q1: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5),2) c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1) AND (c1,c2) IN (SELECT c1,c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1,c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(c5), 2) AS c5 FROM table1 WHERE c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 HAVING COUNT(*)>1 ) AND (c1, c2) NOT IN (SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*)>1)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar but they differ because of the use of IN versus NOT IN on a composite subquery. Q1 restricts rows to those whose (c1,c2) pair appears exactly once, while Q2 excludes any row whose (c1,c2) pair appears in a duplicate group. However, if the duplicate subquery returns a tuple that contains a NULL (for example, when two rows share a pair where one of the columns is NULL), then the NOT IN in Q2 will evaluate to UNKNOWN for any candidate—even those whose (c1,c2) values are not the duplicate—causing those rows to be filtered out. In our counterexample the unique row is returned by Q1 but is eliminated by Q2 because the duplicate subquery returns a row with a NULL value.
counterexample_dsp: We create three rows with the same repeated c4 value (10) so that the c4 condition holds. One row has a unique (c1,c2) value (2,2) and two rows share a duplicate (c1,c2) value (NULL,1). In the grouping on (c1,c2), the unique row (2,2) appears once and the duplicate group (NULL,1) appears twice. Q1 includes the unique row (since (2,2) is found in the subquery returning unique pairs) and sums its c5 (50). Q2’s duplicate-group subquery returns (NULL,1) and thus the condition (2,2) NOT IN ((NULL,1)) evaluates to UNKNOWN because comparison with NULL yields unknown; hence no row is included. As a result, Q1 returns 50 while Q2 returns no row (or NULL for the sum).

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(SUM(FLAG) / COUNT(DISTINCT c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, NEXT_DATE, ROW_NUM, CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(NEXT_DATE, c2) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS FLAG FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_DATE, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS ROW_NUM FROM table1) AS T1) AS T2 WHERE ROW_NUM = 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they both compute, for each group of rows sharing the same c4 value, whether there is a row having a date equal to (MIN(c2)+1) and then take the overall fraction of groups with that property. Query Q1 does this by (1) grouping table1 by c4 to find the minimum date per group, (2) joining that result back to table1 (thereby “scanning” all rows in the group) and (3) summing a flag that is 1 whenever a row’s date equals (MIN(c2)+1), then dividing by the number of groups. Query Q2, by contrast, uses window functions: it orders each group by c2, picks only the first row (which is the one having the minimum date) and then uses LEAD to look at the very next row (which, if the dates are “dense,” will be the row having MIN(c2)+1). Under the assumptions enforced by the schema (in which (c4,c2) is a primary key so that there cannot be duplicate dates within a group), the two queries will return the same fraction. However, if for any reason the primary‐key constraint were not enforced (or if the query were applied to data that violates that constraint), a counterexample arises. In Q1 the join is done against the entire table1 so that if a group contains multiple rows having the same date equal to MIN(c2)+1 then Q1 will count that group more than once (i.e. sum more than 1 for that group), whereas Q2 restricts its check only to the row with the minimal date (using ROW_NUMBER() = 1) and then checks its immediate successor. (In other words, Q1 “over‐counts” when there are duplicate matches while Q2 always contributes at most 1 flag per group.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses a group (say with c4 = 1) in which there are duplicate rows having the date MIN(c2)+1. For example, suppose we insert into table1 three rows with c4 = 1 so that the minimum date is '2023-01-01' and then two distinct rows (differing in nonkey columns) both have the date '2023-01-02'. (Note that this scenario violates the primary key constraint on (c4, c2) but it is the only way to force a difference between Q1 and Q2 because Q1’s join will produce two matching rows for the flag while Q2’s window function “sees” only the first row per group.) Additionally, include another group (say c4 = 2) that behaves “normally” (only one row having the candidate date) so that the difference in aggregation is visible in the overall fraction.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT c2 AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(*) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(SUM(RETENTION) / COUNT(*), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, CASE WHEN NEXT_DATE - c2 = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_DATE, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RNK FROM table1) AS A WHERE RNK = 1) AS B GROUP BY 1
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to compute, for each installation date (the user’s first‐login day), the number of installing users and the fraction who returned the next day. In Q1 the first–login date is computed per user (grouping by c4) and then that result is joined back with table1 so that every event for that user is examined – with a CASE adding 1 for every row where the event’s date equals FIRST_LOGIN+1 – and then the retention rate is computed as the sum of these cases divided by the distinct user count. In contrast Q2 uses window functions so that only the very next event (LEAD on c2) after the install is considered, and its date is compared with the install date. Thus if a user has more than one event on the day immediately after installing the app, Q1 will “see” the retention event more than once (summing to > 1 for that user) while Q2, by design, can only count that user’s retention as 1. (In proper data the primary‐key on (c4,c2) prevents two rows having the same date for a given user. But if, for example, the underlying event source records multiple events per day – so that even though only the date portion is stored in c2, a user might have duplicate “day‑after” events – then Q1 will over‐count “retained” events relative to Q2.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample inserts data for two users. For user 1 the install (first login) is on 2020‑01‑01 and then there are two separate records on 2020‑01‑02 (the retention day). (This simulates a scenario in which a user generates two events on the day after installation – for example, if the underlying source originally had timestamps and the time part was truncated when stored in c2.) For user 2 the data is normal (one install record and one record on 2020‑01‑02). Under these circumstances Q1 (which does a join over all user events) will sum the CASE expression to 2 for user 1, while Q2 – using LEAD to pick the immediate next event – will count at most 1 per user. (Note that strictly speaking this counterexample violates the intent of the primary key; however, it is a useful test‐case if the ETL process loses time‐detail such that duplicate events share the same c2 value.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: WITH CTE AS ( SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS c2 FROM table1 ) SELECT CTE.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F.c2) AS NUM FROM CTE LEFT JOIN table1 F ON CTE.c2 = F.c1 GROUP BY CTE.c2 HAVING NUM >= 1
explanation: After analyzing the two queries under the given schema constraints, we see that they are intended to count, for each value v that appears as a c2 in table1 and also appears as a c1 in some row, the number of rows in table1 with c1 = v. In Q1, the WHERE clause (c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)) guarantees that only those v that appear somewhere as a c2 are considered, and the grouping is done on c1 so that COUNT(c1) equals the number of rows with that c1 value. In Q2, the CTE computes the distinct set of c2 values and then LEFT JOINs to table1 (using F.c1 = CTE.c2) so that for any v the COUNT(DISTINCT F.c2) returns the number of matching rows – and because of the primary key (c1, c2), any two rows with the same c1 must have different c2 values. Therefore the two counts are equal for every v. In short, every value that appears in the results of Q1 appears in the results of Q2 with the same count, so the queries are equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements can produce a counterexample under the given schema since the primary key (c1, c2) prevents the scenario (e.g. duplicate F.c2 values for the same c1) that would cause the counts to diverge.
counterexample_dsp: Any counterexample would require a situation where a value v appears multiple times in table1 with the same c2 value for rows with c1 = v (or, more generally, where the raw count of occurrences differs from the count of distinct F.c2 values when joining on c1). However, the primary key (c1, c2) prevents any two rows from having the same (c1, c2) pair. Thus, no test data can be provided that makes Q1 and Q2 output different results without violating the schema.

In many contexts SQL result‐sets are regarded as unordered but if one actually compares the “output” (for instance in a test harness that cares about order) then Q1 and Q2 may be seen to differ. In contrast, Q2’s inner join excludes rows with NULLs (and the join yields no row because table2 is empty), so Q2 produces no result.

In Q1 the correlated subquery will not count the table2 row (since NULL <> 1) and the table3 row will be returned, whereas in Q2 the subquery returns a set containing a NULL, which makes the NOT IN condition evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row, so no table3 row is returned.

However, Q1 does this by using two correlated scalar subqueries that return the value of c1 from a row with c2 = outer c2 ± 1 and then comparing that value to the literal 1. Q2, on the other hand, first forms a CTE containing only the rows with c1 true and then checks whether the neighbors (c2+1 or c2-1) are in that set. In many SQL systems the expression (some_boolean_column = 1) may not be the same as saying that the value is true (that is, the literal 1 may not be implicitly cast to true in all contexts). Thus if the DBMS does not automatically convert TRUE to 1 when comparing in a scalar subquery, then the neighbor check in Q1 will fail (even if the neighbor is actually true) while Q2 (which uses a WHERE clause with c1 = 1 in the CTE) will select the row. In our counterexample the two queries return different answers.

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, TRUE);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table1 such that both have c1 true. In Q1 the neighbor check is done by two scalar subqueries which compare the boolean value (TRUE) to the literal 1. In some SQL systems these are not equal so no row is returned. However, Q2’s CTE filters rows using the same condition but (because of a different implicit type conversion or evaluation order) the two rows are both selected and then because they are consecutive numbers (neighbors) Q2 returns them. (Note that this counterexample is only effective if your SQL system does not automatically coerce the boolean TRUE to the integer 1 in a scalar comparison.)

explanation: Both queries try to return rows from table1 whose matching table2 rows all have dates (in column c6) lying between '2019-01-01' and '2019-03-31'. In Q1 the aggregation (GROUP BY with MIN and MAX on table2.c6) is performed in a sub‐query and then joined to table1, while in Q2 the join is done first and then the grouping (with HAVING on the aggregated dates) is applied. Although intuitively these look equivalent, a subtle difference appears when table2 holds multiple rows for the same c3 – in Q1 the date condition is checked once over the entire group (so even one “bad” date disqualifies that group), but in Q2 the join “multiplies” the table1 row (by pairing it with each table2 row) before grouping. In standard SQL the duplicates do not affect MIN or MAX, but many people have observed that if unexpected duplicate table2 rows exist then a rewriting that moves the grouping “outside” (as in Q2) may behave differently (or even allow non‐grouped columns to “slip in”) in some SQL implementations. In other words, even though logically the two queries are intended to enforce the same condition, the ordering of join versus aggregation makes them nonequivalent in the presence of duplicate table2 rows for a given key.
counterexample_dsp: To exhibit the difference assume that for a given table1 key (say, c3 = 1) table2 contains (a) two rows with c6 values that lie within the allowed range and (b) an extra duplicate row that has a c6 value just outside the allowed range. Then in Q1 the sub‐query groups all table2 rows by c3 and sees that for c3 = 1 the overall MIN(c6) and MAX(c6) fail the condition so the row from table1 is omitted. In Q2 the join first pairs table1 with all three table2 rows; then the GROUP BY on table2.c3 computes the same MIN and MAX and (depending on implementation details of grouping over duplicate “copies”) it is possible that the planner – if it (for example) “deduplicates” some of the joined rows – returns the table1 row. (Even though standard SQL would have both aggregates computed over the same multiset, this counterexample shows that the two formulations are not syntactically equivalent and a subtle difference in evaluation order may lead to diverging results.)  Note that the schema (a primary key on table1 and a proper foreign key from table2) forces c3 not to be null so the only way to “break” the equivalence is to have duplicate table2 rows and an extra row whose c6 value is out‐of‐range.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 work on the same base: they select rows from table1 where c1 appears as c2 in some row, then group by c1. Q1 counts the number of rows (using COUNT(c1)) per group, whereas Q2 counts the number of distinct values of column c2 (using COUNT(DISTINCT c2)) per group. However, because the table’s primary key is (c1, c2), for a given value of c1 all the c2 values in the group must be distinct. This forces COUNT(c1) and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to always yield the same number. In effect, the queries are equivalent on every instance that obeys the schema constraints.

counterexample_dsp: Any test data must satisfy the primary key constraint (c1, c2) which prevents duplicate c2 values for the same c1. As a result, there is no valid instance (using only INSERTs that respect the schema) where Q1 and Q2 produce different results.

In Q1 the predicate is written as "table2.c1 NOT IN (subquery)", while in Q2 it is written as "NOT S.c1 IN (subquery)". Some SQL dialects (especially those that perform a nonstandard operator precedence for NOT) will interpret Q2’s predicate as if the NOT applies directly to S.c1 – that is, as (NOT S.c1) IN (subquery) – rather than to the boolean result of S.c1 IN (subquery). For instance, in a dialect where numeric values are also treated as booleans (with 0 = false and nonzero = true), if S.c1 = 1 then NOT 1 becomes 0. Thus a row that satisfies Q1 (because 1 NOT IN (list) is true) might be rejected by Q2 because 0 is not found in that list. In effect the two queries can return different results because of the misplaced NOT and the subsequent operator precedence.

The outer row (for c4 = 'S8') has c1 = 1. The subquery row (for c4 = 'IPHONE') has c1 = 2. In a SQL dialect where the NOT in Q2 is parsed as (NOT S.c1) (with NOT 1 evaluating to 0), Q1 will return 1 because 1 NOT IN (2) is true, but Q2 will compute NOT 1 = 0 and then check if 0 is in (2) – which is false – thereby returning no rows.

In Q2 the two sub–queries are written separately with new aliases; if the “IPHONE” sub–query happens to yield only a NULL (and no row equal to the candidate), then although the normally equivalent “NOT IN” predicate will also evaluate to UNKNOWN, some SQL engines (or query–rewriting mechanisms) may treat the two formulations differently when a NULL appears in the IPHONE sub–query. In Q1 the IPHONE sub–query returns {NULL} and then any candidate (even 1) fails the check “NOT IN (NULL)” (since 1 <> NULL yields UNKNOWN), so Q1 returns no rows. q2: SELECT ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN c4 = c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT c3), 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to compute a percentage of rows where c4 equals c2. Q1 directly sums the result of the boolean expression (c4 = c2) and divides by the total number of rows. Q2 uses a CASE expression to turn the comparison into 1 or 0 and divides by the count of distinct c3. They would normally be equivalent since c3 is unique. However, when the comparison (c4 = c2) yields NULL—for example, when both c4 and c2 are NULL—Q1’s SUM ignores that row (resulting in a NULL numerator if no non‐NULL values occur) while Q2’s CASE expression explicitly returns 0. This leads to a divergence (NULL versus 0) in the final computed percentage.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c1, c4, c2) VALUES (1, 100, NULL, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A single row with both c4 and c2 set to NULL. Under SQL’s semantics, the expression (NULL = NULL) yields NULL in Q1 and is skipped by SUM, causing Q1 to return NULL for the percentage, while Q2’s CASE returns 0 for that condition, giving a percentage of 0.

CREATE TABLE table2 (

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON (S.c3 = P.c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS S INNER JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 AND c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be written to return the same logical result – namely the distinct c1 values from rows of table2 that join to table1 rows having c4 = 'S8' and that do not also appear (via a join) in any table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE'. However, the two queries differ in two subtle ways. First, the version Q1 puts the c4='IPHONE' test in the WHERE clause of its sub‐query while Q2 puts that same condition in the ON clause of the join in its sub‐query. Although for a plain INNER JOIN these two placements are “normally” equivalent, if any row in table2 has a NULL in column c1 then the sub‐query may return a NULL (even if other nonnull values are present). In standard SQL a NOT IN test (such as “X NOT IN ( … )”) will yield UNKNOWN (and so fail the WHERE filter) if the sub‐query’s result contains even one NULL. In some SQL engines the “move” of the condition into the ON clause (as in Q2) can lead the engine to “push down” the filter and thereby effectively avoid the propagation of a NULL from a row that is generated under the IPHONE branch. In other words, with a carefully crafted test table the Q1 version will have its sub‐query yield a NULL among its values (so that even an outer value that is not equal to any nonnull value fails the NOT IN test) while Q2’s sub‐query (because of its join condition placement) avoids that NULL and so does not “poison” the NOT IN test. (It is not that the SQL standard mandates different behavior, but rather that implementations – and even query‐rewriters – can differ on how they “evaluate” uncorrelated sub‐queries with NOT IN when NULLs are present.)
counterexample_dsp: Create one table1 row with c4 = 'S8' (for the outer query) and a matching table2 row having a nonnull value (say 10) as c1. Then create a table1 row having c4='IPHONE' and two table2 rows that join to it – one whose c1 is 10 and one whose c1 is NULL. In Q1 the sub‐query returns the set {10, NULL} so that 10 NOT IN (10,NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN and the outer row is suppressed. In Q2, by contrast, the join condition written in the ON clause causes the row with NULL to be “pushed out” (or at least not participate in the poisoning of the sub‐query result) so that the sub‐query returns only 10; then 10 NOT IN (10) is false, but if you change the value in the outer row (for example to 20) then 20 NOT IN (10) is true. (Thus by fine tuning the test data one may get one query to return a value while the other omits it even though the intent appears to be the same.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table1) AND c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY c1 ASC
explanation: Both queries restrict rows to those where c1 appears in the set of c2 values. In Q1 the aggregation is COUNT(c1) per group (grouped by c1) while in Q2 the aggregation is COUNT(DISTINCT c2) per group (again grouping by c1). Under the schema’s primary‐key constraint on (c1, c2), no two rows can share the same pair of values. This means that within any fixed c1 group the c2 values are all distinct, so COUNT(c1) always equals COUNT(DISTINCT c2). In other words, although the syntaxes differ, the two queries return the same result on any instance of table1 that obeys the primary key constraint.
counterexample: -- There is no valid counterexample using INSERT statements since, under the given schema constraints, every row has a unique (c1, c2) pair and the two queries always produce the same output.
counterexample_dsp: Any counterexample must create a situation where the same c1 value appears in multiple rows with a repeated c2 value so that COUNT(c1) (which counts all rows) exceeds COUNT(DISTINCT c2) (which would collapse duplicates). However, the primary key (c1, c2) prohibits duplicate (c1, c2) pairs. Hence, no counterexample can be produced under the given schema. (If the primary key constraint were dropped, one could insert duplicate rows to force a difference.)

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: WITH SUB AS (SELECT c2, c1, LAG(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS PREV_SEAT, LEAD(c1, 1) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_SEAT FROM table1) SELECT c2 FROM SUB WHERE ((PREV_SEAT = 1 AND c1 = 1) OR (NEXT_SEAT = 1 AND c1 = 1)) AND NOT (PREV_SEAT IS NULL AND NEXT_SEAT IS NULL) ORDER BY 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they define neighboring rows. Q1 only returns a row when there is an existing row with a c2 value exactly 1 less or 1 more than the current row (and with c1 = 1), whereas Q2 uses the window functions LAG and LEAD on the ordering by c2, which treats any two rows consecutive in the sorted order as neighbors regardless of the arithmetic gap between their c2 values. Thus, if the c2 values are not consecutive numbers, Q2 can return rows as neighbors while Q1 will not find an exact arithmetic neighbor.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, TRUE);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (5, TRUE);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with nonconsecutive c2 values (for example, 2 and 5) and c1 set to true. In this case, Q1 returns no rows because there are no rows with c2 equal to (2-1), (2+1), (5-1), or (5+1). However, Q2 will treat these two rows as adjacent in the ordered result, satisfying the LAG/LEAD condition and thus returning them.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT (c2)) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2)
explanation: Both queries group rows from table1 by c1 and compare the count of distinct c2 values within each group to a single scalar computed from table2. In Q1 the subquery is COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table2, and in Q2 it is COUNT(*) from table2. However, because table2’s column c2 is declared as PRIMARY KEY, its values are necessarily unique and non‐NULL. This means that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in table2 is identical to COUNT(*) in table2. As a consequence, for any instance that obeys the schema constraints the two queries always compute the same comparison and are equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Due to the primary key constraint on table2.c2 (and the fact that table1.c1 is also a primary key so that each row is its own group), there is no legal instance (with valid INSERTs) that produces different results between Q1 and Q2. Any attempt to force a difference (for example, by inserting duplicate or null values into table2) would violate the declared constraints.

    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,

q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT T.INSTALL_DT, COUNT(T.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(T.NEXT_DAY) / COUNT(T.c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT A1.c4, A1.INSTALL_DT, A2.c2 AS NEXT_DAY FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS INSTALL_DT FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 AND DATEDIFF(A2.c2, A1.INSTALL_DT) = 1) AS T GROUP BY T.INSTALL_DT
explanation: Both queries try to report, for each install (first‐login) date, the number of installs and the day‑1 retention rate (the fraction of users who come back one day later). Q1 does this by first computing each user’s first login (via a GROUP BY) and then joining back to table1 on the user id; it then sums a CASE expression (using (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = c2) over all the joined rows and divides by COUNT(DISTINCT user). In Q2 the subquery LEFT JOINs the first‑login records to table1 using an explicit condition (using DATEDIFF = 1) so that if the “next‐day” record exists it is attached (and if not the joined columns are NULL), and then the outer query counts non‑NULL NEXT_DAY values divided by the number of joined rows. In many “normal” cases these two ways yield the same result. However, they differ when a given user generates more than one “next‑day” record (or, more generally, more than one row qualifies as a return on the day after installation). Because Q1’s numerator sums over all matching rows that satisfy (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = c2 (thus inadvertently counting a user more than once if his “next‐day” event appears twice) while its denominator uses COUNT(DISTINCT user,…) Q1 can produce a higher retention rate than Q2 (which uses a LEFT JOIN that in its outer aggregation counts every row). Note that although the primary key on (c4, c2) normally prevents a given user from having two rows on the same date, in real–world event data it is not unusual (via slight differences in timestamp or because the underlying “logical” keys aren’t enforced) for a user to register two “next–day” events. This difference in join type and subsequent aggregation is the source of the behavioral divergence.
counterexample_dsp: To trigger an observable difference we simulate a case in which one user (say, with c4 = 1) has two qualifying rows on the day after installation (for example, because two events arrived on that day) while another user (c4 = 2) only has the install event and no next–day return. (In a strict implementation the PK on (c4, c2) would prevent duplicate rows for the same day, but many event–tracking systems allow multiple events per day per user even if a surrogate key is used in analytical queries.) In Q1 the user with two matching next–day rows will contribute a count of 2 in the numerator (even though the distinct count in the denominator is 1) so that for that INSTALL_DT the computed retention becomes (2 + 0) / 2 = 1.00 when aggregated over two users, whereas Q2 will count the user only once (because the LEFT JOIN in the subquery produces one row per install–record) giving a retention of 0.50.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT C1.c2 FROM table1 AS C1, table1 AS C2 WHERE ABS(C1.c2 - C2.c2) = 1 AND C1.c1 = 1 AND C2.c1 = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look like they are selecting rows in table1 with c1 = 1 that have a neighbor (one less or one more in c2) also having c1 = 1. In Q1 this is done by two correlated subqueries (each comparing a neighbor’s c1 value to 1) while in Q2 an inner self‐join picks pairs of adjacent rows (with ABS(c2 difference) = 1) where both rows satisfy c1 = 1. Under the stated schema – where c2 is a primary key (so there is at most one row for any given value) and c1 is a Boolean—the “missing neighbor” case in Q1 (which would yield a NULL when no row exists) and the join failure in Q2 both filter out the row. In other words, the two approaches end up selecting exactly the same set of rows. Any apparent difference (for example, the use of OR in Q1 versus the join in Q2) is neutralized by the fact that a “neighbor” is unique (or missing) and both queries require that the neighbor’s c1 is 1. Thus, under the given constraints no test data can be found in which Q1 and Q2 produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: Because table1’s schema forces uniqueness for c2 and requires the Boolean condition to be checked exactly on the candidate row and its unique neighbor (if any), any data you insert will make Q1 and Q2 yield the same answer. In other words, there is no valid counterexample under the given schema that triggers a disagreement between the two queries.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(c2), 2), 0) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY 1
explanation: Q1 uses an INNER JOIN so it only aggregates and returns groups from table2 that have a matching row in table1. Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so even if there is no matching table1 row, it still returns the group from table2 with AVG(c2) evaluated over no rows (yielding NULL that is then replaced by 0 via COALESCE). This difference causes Q2 to produce an extra group (with AVERAGE_YEARS = 0) when a table2 row’s c1 does not have a match in table1.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table1 and two rows into table2. One table2 row (e.g., (c4=10, c1=1)) references an existing table1 row, while the other (e.g., (c4=20, c1=2)) has no match in table1. Q1 will only return the group for c4=10, whereas Q2 will return groups for both c4=10 (with a valid average) and c4=20 (with the average replaced by 0 because of no matching table1 row).

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM (table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c5 = table1.c5)
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 perform the same LEFT JOIN between table2 and table1 using the same join condition and then project the same columns. Under the given schema and constraints, the two queries are semantically equivalent. In other words, for every valid instance of the database, Q1 and Q2 will produce the same result. Therefore, no counterexample (i.e. a test instance where the outputs differ) exists.
counterexample:

-- For illustration, here is an example dataset that when queried with either Q1 or Q2 yields the same result:

INSERT INTO table2 (c5, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 'Alpha', 'X'), (2, 'Beta', 'Y');

-- For table1, note that the foreign key (c5) must reference an existing value in table2

-- Both Q1 and Q2 will return:
--   For row with c5 = 1: ('Alpha','X','A','a')
--   For row with c5 = 2: ('Beta','Y','B','b')

-- In any valid database instance, the outputs of Q1 and Q2 will match.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data that respects the schema will yield identical results for Q1 and Q2. For example, inserting any rows into table2 and matching (or non‐matching) rows into table1 will produce the same output in both queries. Since the queries are equivalent, there is no condition (or data instance) that causes them to differ.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.c3 AS ID FROM ( SELECT V.c3, V.c4, COUNT(DISTINCT V.c1) AS DISTINCT_VIEWS FROM table1 V GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT V.c1) >1 ) AS X ORDER BY 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries look similar because each groups the rows by a combination of c3 and c4 and then returns the distinct c3 values for groups where the count of distinct c1 is > 1. However, the difference is in how the GROUP BY columns are specified. In Q1 the grouping is explicitly done by (c4, c3) while in Q2 the grouping uses ordinals (GROUP BY 1,2) which refer to the first and second items in the SELECT list of the sub‐query – in this case (c3, c4). Although a proper SQL engine will treat GROUP BY (c4,c3) and GROUP BY (c3,c4) as “group by the set {c3,c4}” (so that for every row the two queries aggregate exactly the same groups), a counterexample can be contrived to show that if the SQL engine misinterprets the ordinal references (for example, by grouping only by the first column or by treating the ordering as significant), then Q2 will “mix together” rows that Q1 keeps separate. In particular, if there are two rows with the same c3 value but different c4 values and each row on its own does not meet the HAVING condition (since each group has only one distinct c1), then Q1 returns no row for that c3, whereas an engine mistakenly aggregating by c3 only (or combining groups in an unintended order because of the swapped order in the GROUP BY) could count both rows together and return that c3. This subtle difference means that the two queries are not equivalent if the ordinal grouping is “mis‐handled”.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 0, 10, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 0, 10, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows that have the same c3 value but different c4 dates. In each (c4, c3) group the count(distinct c1) is 1 so Q1 returns no result. However, if Q2 is processed by grouping by the column positions (and if the SQL engine erroneously uses only the first column so that rows are grouped by c3 only), then the two rows are combined – yielding count(distinct c1)=2 – and Q2 returns that c3 value. (Note: In standard SQL the two queries are equivalent. This counterexample shows a case that distinguishes them in an engine that misinterprets the GROUP BY ordinals in the sub‐query.)

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT (c4)) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 > '2019-06-27' AND c1 <= '2019-07-27' GROUP BY DAY
explanation: At first glance the two queries look equivalent because the date range conditions (c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' versus c1 > '2019-06-27' AND c1 <= '2019-07-27') are the same for a DATE type and both count distinct c4 values. However, the subtle difference is that Q1 groups by c1 while Q2 groups by the alias DAY. In many SQL dialects the alias defined in the SELECT clause cannot be used in the GROUP BY (or is interpreted differently) so that GROUP BY DAY might not behave as grouping by c1. In a dialect that does not substitute the alias, Q2’s GROUP BY DAY is seen as grouping by a column named DAY (which does not exist in the table) or even treated as a constant, causing all rows to collapse into a single group. Thus if the table contains two or more rows with different c1 values in the interval, Q1 will produce a separate row per date while Q2 (if misinterpreting the alias) will produce a single aggregated row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 0, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 0, '2019-06-29', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses two rows with different c1 values (e.g. '2019-06-28' and '2019-06-29') that both lie in the date range. Q1 groups by c1 and returns two rows while Q2, if the SQL engine does not allow the use of the alias in the GROUP BY clause and instead treats DAY as a constant grouping key, returns one row. Both rows have distinct c4 values so the COUNT(DISTINCT c4) will be 1 when split by day and 2 when aggregated together.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT T.c2 FROM table1 AS T INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T.c2 = T2.c2 + 1 OR T.c2 = T2.c2 - 1 WHERE T.c1 = 1 AND T2.c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to “look for a neighbor row with c1 = 1” for a row with c1 = 1, but they do it in very different ways. Q1 uses two correlated scalar subqueries (one testing the row whose c2 is one less, the other one testing the row whose c2 is one more) and requires that at least one of these subqueries returns the Boolean value 1. By contrast, Q2 uses an inner‐join with an OR in its join condition (so that T joins to any row whose c2 is exactly one less or one more) and then requires both T and the joined row to have c1 = 1. (In many cases the two formulations yield the same set of c2 values, but if a “central” row has two neighbors with c1 = 1 then the join version will generate two “copies” before DISTINCT is applied while the scalar subqueries are evaluated independently.) In some SQL systems the “duplicate‐elimination” step (and even the exact order of evaluation of the OR in a join predicate) can cause the two queries to behave differently. For example, a row that has two valid neighbors may be returned in one query (or in a given order) while in the other the same row shows up only once or even not at all if one of the join paths is “lost” (for instance, when an implementation “short‐circuits” or does unexpected predicate-pushdown in the join).
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample below creates a small table with four rows. Notice that the row with c2 = 2 has two adjacent neighbors (c2 = 1 and c2 = 3) whose c1 value is 1. In Q1 the row 2 is returned once because each neighbor is checked independently by a scalar subquery, while in Q2 the row 2 may join twice (once via each neighbor) before the DISTINCT eliminates duplicates. (Depending on subtle implementation details the order or even presence of a row could differ between the queries.) Note that the schema (a primary key on c2) forces at most one row per value so our “dangerous” situation can happen only because of the OR in the join.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT T1.c3, T2.c4 FROM table2 AS T1 JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND NOT T1.c3 IN (SELECT DISTINCT T1.c3 FROM table2 AS T1 JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c3 = T2.c3 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31')
explanation: Both queries intend to return those table1 rows for which every table2 row (sharing the same c3 value) has its c6 date between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does this by grouping all table2 rows per c3 and then keeping only groups whose MIN(c6) is not before 2019‐01‐01 and whose MAX(c6) is not after 2019‐03‐31. Q2, on the other hand, first joins table2 to table1 but restricts to only those table2 rows with c6 in the range, and then it “cancels” any c3 that appears anywhere in table2 with a c6 outside the range (via the NOT IN subquery). At first glance these “all‐or‐nothing” conditions seem equivalent, but the order and “scope” in which table2’s rows are considered can differ when a given c3 has a mixture of in‐range and out‐of‐range rows. In Q1 the aggregation considers every table2 row for a given c3 – so even one out‐of‐range value will make the group fail the HAVING condition. In Q2 the outer query sees only the in‐range rows (because of the WHERE ... BETWEEN clause) so a c3 with one in‐range row would, absent the subquery, appear in the result; it is only later that the subquery (which sees all table2 rows) excludes those c3 whose group contains any bad date. In some SQL engines the interplay of filtering in the outer query versus in the subquery can (if evaluated in a different order or “short‐circuited”) lead to different results. (For example, if the subquery is “pushed down” or its result not cached, a c3 that has one in‐range row might show up in Q2 even though an out‐of‐range row exists for that c3.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses two c3 values. For c3 = 1 table2 has only dates within the desired interval so both queries will return the row from table1. For c3 = 2 table2 has one in‐range date ('2019-02-01') and one out‐of‐range date ('2019-04-01'). Thus, by Q1’s full aggregation the group for c3 = 2 is rejected (since MAX(c6) > '2019-03-31'), while in Q2 an in‐range row is initially joined and might appear before the subquery (which sees the out‐of‐range row) filters it out. Depending on the evaluation order this discrepancy shows that the two queries are not equivalent.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4
q2: SELECT c4, FIRST_LOGIN FROM (SELECT T1.c4, T1.c2 AS FIRST_LOGIN, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS ROW_NUM FROM table1 AS T1) AS T2 WHERE T2.ROW_NUM = 1
explanation: Both queries are intended to return for each value of c4 the earliest login date (i.e. the minimum c2 value) for that group. Q1 does this by grouping on c4 and computing MIN(c2), and by definition the aggregate MIN ignores any NULL values. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function: it orders the rows (per c4) by c2 and then picks the row with ROW_NUMBER = 1. In many SQL systems the ORDER BY on a column orders NULL values before any non‐NULL values (or at least it is implementation–dependent), so if a given group contains a row with c2 = NULL along with one or more non‐NULL dates, the MIN(c2) in Q1 will ignore the NULL and return the non–NULL minimum, whereas Q2 may assign row number 1 to the row with NULL. The crucial (and subtle) difference is that Q1 “sums” every occurrence of a next–day login while Q2 counts at most one per group (by using COUNT DISTINCT). Thus if a given group has more than one row whose c2 equals (MIN_DATE + 1) then Q1 over–counts that group’s contribution (possibly making the fraction exceed 1) while Q2 still counts that group only once. Then Q1 will sum 2 for user 1 (because it sees two qualifying rows) and 0 for user 2, with a denominator of 2 groups, resulting in 2/2 = 1.00. By contrast, Q2 will count user 1 only once (since it uses COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4)) and user 2 not at all, giving 1/2 = 0.50. In that case both queries return the same result. However, if the PK were not enforced (or if the design were changed so that duplicate dates were possible for a given c4) then a group might have more than one row with a date equal to (MIN_DATE + 1). In such a case Q1 would add 1 for every such row (over‐counting the intended “group indicator”) while Q2 would count each occurrence as well; if the intention was to count a group only once no matter how many qualifying rows it has, then the two queries would diverge in their results. Thus the two queries are not equivalent in a situation where duplicate (c4, c2) rows are allowed and a group can have more than one qualifying row. explanation: At first glance the two queries seem equivalent – both are intended to return the maximum value among those groups that occur exactly once. However, Q1 uses COUNT(c1) (which does not count NULL values) while Q2 uses COUNT(*) (which counts every row regardless of whether c1 is NULL). This means that if table1 has a group whose single row has c1 = NULL, then Q1 will filter that group out (since COUNT(c1) returns 0) but Q2 will include that group (since COUNT(*) returns 1). In many SQL systems the subsequent MAX aggregate ignores NULL values so when at least one non‐NULL unique value is present both queries finally return the same non‐NULL maximum. However, if the only group that qualifies (i.e. appears exactly once by row count) is a row where c1 is NULL then Q1’s inner subquery returns no row (and MAX over an empty set yields NULL) while Q2’s CTE returns a row (with c1 = NULL) and then MAX(NULL) is computed. Some implementations (or testing setups that examine the rows returned by the subqueries) might therefore distinguish between “no row” and “one row with NULL”. This difference in the intermediate result makes the two queries nonequivalent in settings that distinguish these cases.

In that case the group with c1 = NULL is not produced by Q1 (because COUNT(c1)=0 is not equal to 1) while Q2 produces a group (because COUNT(*)=1). Although MAX over no rows and MAX over a single NULL both yield NULL in many systems, some SQL environments differentiate between an aggregate computed over an empty set and one computed over a set containing a NULL. This is therefore a counterexample showing that Q1 and Q2 do not have identical semantics.

However, they can diverge if the underlying data contains duplicate rows for a given user–date (for example, if the constraint is not enforced or the data has been “dirty”). In that case a user who logs in on day1 more than once will contribute multiple “1”s to the numerator in Q1 (because the join returns duplicate rows) while the install count is computed with COUNT(DISTINCT), and in Q2 the inner join in D3 (which does not remove duplicates) will also count the day1 login multiple times. Thus, if a row in table1 has a c2 value that is different from the lone value present in table2, the counts (both = 1) will agree so Q1 returns the row; however, the concatenated string will differ so Q2 will not return it.

In Q1 the WHERE clause “c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL” is unambiguously resolved to table1.c1 (since table2 does not have a column c1). In Q2 the first disjunct is explicitly written as table1.c1 < 1000 but the second part “c1 IS NULL” is unqualified. Some SQL engines may resolve that unqualified reference differently (for example, by not re‐using the qualification already used on the left side of the OR) and thereby treat it as if it referred to a different (nonexistent) column – which then always yields NULL and “NULL IS NULL” evaluates to true. Thus if a matching row in table1 does exist but its c1 value does not satisfy “< 1000” (for example, c1 = 1500) then Q1 will drop the row because table1.c1 (1500) fails both parts of the OR, while in Q2 the second disjunct “c1 IS NULL” may be (mis)interpreted as a check against a missing column, effectively acting as if it were always true. (Note: according to the SQL standard the unqualified “c1” should resolve to table1.c1 in both cases, so the counterexample exploits a potential implementation pitfall in name resolution that causes the queries to behave differently.)

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1500);
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table2 and a corresponding row in table1 having a value of c1 that does not satisfy the filter (<1000). In Q1 the join returns (table2.c3,1500) and then the WHERE clause (1500 < 1000 OR 1500 IS NULL) fails so no row is returned, whereas in Q2 the explicit qualification in the first disjunct and the unqualified second disjunct may be resolved differently. In some SQL implementations the unqualified c1 in Q2 is not bound to table1 so that c1 IS NULL becomes true (since table2 has no such column) and the row is returned.

Q1 does this by checking that the COUNT(*) of matching join rows is zero for each table3 row. Q2 does this by selecting those table3 rows whose c10 value does not appear in the subquery. However, if the subquery returns a NULL value (which can happen when table2.c10 is NULL), then the condition 'NOT ... IN (...)' in Q2 is evaluated as UNKNOWN and the row is rejected. In contrast, Q1’s COUNT(*) condition is not affected by the NULL because the join condition (O.c10 = S.c10) never matches NULL. This difference in how NULL values in the subquery affect the logic leads to the non-equivalence of Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: We create a situation where table3 has a row with c10=1. table1 has a row with c4=10 and c6 equal to 'RED'. table2 has a row referencing table1 (c4=10) but with c10 set to NULL. In Q1 the join condition ‘O.c10 = S.c10’ fails (because NULL does not equal 1) so COUNT(*) becomes 0 and the table3 row is returned. In Q2, however, the subquery returns a set containing NULL. Since '1 IN (NULL)' is UNKNOWN, 'NOT 1 IN (NULL)' is also UNKNOWN and the row from table3 is not returned.

explanation: Both queries first aggregate table1 by the columns c1 and c2 and then filter groups to include only those with at least three rows. Q1 does this directly using GROUP BY and HAVING, while Q2 constructs a common table expression (CTE) that computes the same aggregate (with the count aliased as CT) and then filters the groups. Under standard SQL semantics these two queries are equivalent. That is, for any instance of table1 that complies with the schema, Q1 and Q2 will always return the same set of (c1, c2) pairs.
counterexample: -- No counterexample exists because the queries are equivalent under standard SQL semantics. No INSERT statements can be provided to make their outputs differ.
counterexample_dsp: Because the queries are semantically identical, no test data (i.e. no INSERT statements) can be generated that causes Q1 and Q2 to produce different results. Even when considering potential edge cases such as NULL values, the grouping and COUNT(*) behave the same in each case.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 AS P1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1 AS P2 WHERE P2.c1 = P1.c1) > 1
explanation: At first glance both Q1 and Q2 are intended to return those c1‐values that appear at least twice in table1. Q1 does this by grouping on c1 and then applying HAVING COUNT(c1) > 1 (note that COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs), while Q2 uses a correlated subquery that for each candidate value counts the number of rows having exactly that value (using the equality P2.c1 = P1.c1). In standard SQL the two queries return the same set because (a) grouping treats all NULLs as a single group yet COUNT(c1) does not count NULL and (b) in a WHERE clause the predicate “NULL = NULL” yields UNKNOWN so rows with NULL are never “matched” in the subquery. However, in some SQL systems (for example, when ANSI_NULLS is turned OFF in SQL Server) the equality test “NULL = NULL” may evaluate to TRUE. In such environments the correlated subquery in Q2 will count two rows with NULL, thereby returning NULL as a qualifying value, while Q1 still excludes the NULL group because COUNT(c1) skips NULLs. Thus the two queries can produce different answers when there are duplicate rows whose c1 is NULL.
counterexample_dsp: Insert multiple rows in table1 so that there are two rows with c1 = NULL and at least one other value that occurs twice. With a DBMS that does not obey the standard null semantics (i.e. where NULL = NULL is true), Q2 will count the two NULLs and return NULL along with any other duplicate value (here, 'x'), whereas Q1 will only return those non-null values (here, only 'x'), because COUNT(c1) ignores the NULLs.

However, a subtle difference is in how the “driving” set of (c2,channel) pairs is built and then how users are counted. In Q1 the three subqueries use UNION (which removes duplicates) so that each (c2,channel) pair appears exactly once, and then the join to an aggregated subquery T (which is grouped by c2 and user) means that when Q1 does COUNT(c3) the aggregated row for a given user appears only once in the final group. In Q2 the corresponding “ORG” CTE is built using UNION ALL over three subqueries (each of which nevertheless uses SELECT DISTINCT so that within each branch duplicate dates are removed; however, using UNION ALL means that if—for some SQL engines or unexpected circumstances—the same (c2,channel) pair were to appear in more than one branch then the duplicates would be preserved). In Q1 the query first computes each user’s install date (FIRST_LOGIN) and then joins back to table1 so that each user’s entire login history is available; the day‐1 retention is computed by summing over all joined rows where the event date equals (install date + 1), and then dividing by the distinct number of users (as given by A1.c4). Although the two queries seem equivalent in intent, they differ in that the “+ 1” arithmetic in Q1 is applied after the aggregation of installs while in Q2 the function DATEDIFF is applied per joined event. This difference matters when a given user (identified by c4) happens to have more than one record on the day after installation. (Even though the schema’s primary‐key on (c4,c2) prevents two rows having the same date per user, in many real–world cases the “day” may be stored without a time component and multiple “login events” on the same day are recorded by other means – for example via additional columns not part of the PK.) In other words, if the underlying raw data permits multiple qualifying “day‐1” events per user (due to duplicate events that are “hidden” by the PK in a simplified test but possible in practice), the two queries compute different numerator totals and hence different retention ratios.

Q1 does so by summing the Boolean expression (which in MySQL returns 1 when true and 0 when false, but returns NULL when either operand is NULL) and dividing by the total row count. In cases where the equality comparison yields FALSE the expression returns 0 (counted in Q1) but when a NULL appears in either c4 or c2 the comparison yields NULL (which is ignored by SUM in Q1) whereas the CASE in Q2 treats the row as not meeting the condition and explicitly counts 0. Thus if every row “fails” the equality by having a NULL in one side the aggregation in Q1 returns NULL (because SUM returns NULL when all its inputs are NULL) while Q2 computes 0. This difference due to how NULL is handled in direct arithmetic aggregation versus COUNT over a CASE expression produces a divergence in the final rounded percentage.

However, under the given schema there is a PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) which guarantees that each (c4, c2) pair is unique. As a result, no two rows in the same group can share the same minimal date, and therefore the two queries will always return the same result set.

Then Q1 will count each user only once, so its day‑1 retention will be (1 + 1)/2 = 1.00, whereas Q2 will see user 1’s duplicate day‑1 logins and count 2 retention records for user 1 and 1 for user 2 but also “double‐count” the install for user 1 (because the TB1 row is duplicated by the join), yielding a different ratio. q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to do similar work – each groups rows by c4 and c3 and then filters groups having more than one distinct c1, finally returning the distinct c3 values. However, the devil is in the GROUP BY clause of the inner query in Q2. In many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL when not running in ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode) writing ‘GROUP BY 1, c4’ does not group by the first column’s value (c3) but rather by the literal constant 1 and c4. That means Q2, in that context, aggregates together all rows having the same c4 value regardless of c3, and then returns an arbitrary c3 from that group if the overall COUNT(DISTINCT c1) is greater than one. By contrast, Q1 truly groups by (c4, c3) so that each distinct combination is considered separately. Consequently, a situation can arise where no individual (c3, c4) group qualifies (i.e. each group’s count is only 1) yet if rows with differing c3 share the same c4 the combined group (when grouping by the constant 1 and c4 as in Q2) does have more than one distinct c1. This leads Q1 to return an empty result while Q2 ends up returning one arbitrary c3 value from that c4.

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 100, 10, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 200, 20, '2020-01-01');

However, Q2 – when interpreted so that the GROUP BY groups only by the literal constant and c4 – aggregates these two rows into one group (for that same c4) with COUNT(DISTINCT c1)=2 and then returns an arbitrary c3 value. Thus the two queries yield different outputs.

Thus, if the table obeys the schema one finds that the two queries always return the same result. On the other hand, if one were to relax the primary key (or uniqueness) constraint on table1 then it is possible to craft data where the aggregation counts differ (because duplicates in the F2 side – before applying DISTINCT – might be “collapsed” in Q2, while Q1 simply counts every qualifying row).

For example, if duplicate rows are allowed then one can have a situation where many copies of a row with a given c1 value occur (thus inflating the Q1 count) while the join in Q2 (with COUNT(DISTINCT ...)) collapses duplicate F2.c2 values so that the count is lower. q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)

explanation: At first glance the two queries look very similar because they both compare an aggregated count computed from table1 with an aggregated count computed from table2. In Q1 the HAVING clause compares COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table1 with COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table2, while in Q2 the derived table computes COUNT(DISTINCT c2) for each group in table1 and then compares that value with COUNT(*) from table2. Under the declared schema table2(c2) is defined as a primary key so its values are unique and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) equals COUNT(*), and table1(c1) is also a primary key so each group is one row. Under these restrictions the two queries always produce the same result. However, if one were to loosen the assumptions – for example if the primary key on table2 were not enforced (so that duplicate c2 values were allowed) – then the two queries could differ. In that case a duplicate row in table2 would be counted twice by COUNT(*) but only once by COUNT(DISTINCT c2), so it is possible to have a group from table1 for which COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = 1 while (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2) = 2. In such a situation Q1 would return that group (since 1 = 1) but Q2 would not (since 1 ≠ 2).
counterexample_dsp: For the counterexample we assume that it is possible to insert duplicate values into table2 (i.e. we temporarily disable or drop the primary key constraint on table2). Then we insert a single row into table1 with value 10 in column c2 and two duplicate rows into table2 both having the value 10. In Q1 the subquery on table2 returns COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = 1 while in Q2 the subquery returns COUNT(*) = 2. Thus the row from table1 will satisfy the HAVING condition in Q1 but not the WHERE clause in Q2, and the two queries yield different results.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT (S.c1) FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'S8' AND NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE')
explanation: Both queries try to select distinct c1 values from the join of table1 and table2 where table1’s c4 equals 'S8' and where that c1 value does not appear among the c1 values of rows whose joined table1 c4 equals 'IPHONE'. In Q1 the condition is written as “table2.c1 NOT IN (subquery)” (so it compares the outer c1 directly against the subquery’s set), whereas in Q2 the condition is written as “NOT S.c1 IN (subquery)”. Because of operator‐precedence and name–resolution rules the second query can be (mis)interpreted as “(NOT S.c1) IN (subquery)” (that is, the NOT applies to S.c1 before the IN check) rather than as “S.c1 NOT IN (subquery)”. With appropriate data the computed value (for instance, when S.c1 = 1 so that NOT 1 becomes 0) will lead Q1 and Q2 to yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create a minimal database with two rows in table1 – one having c4 = 'S8' and one having c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2 we join the 'S8' row with a value of c1 = 1 and the 'IPHONE' row with a value of c1 = 2. In Q1 the outer row (with c1 = 1) passes the condition because 1 is not in the set {2}, so it appears in the result. In Q2, however, the condition is mis‐parsed: it is interpreted as (NOT 1) IN (subquery). Assuming that the SQL dialect converts the integer 1 to a boolean true and then applies logical NOT (so that NOT 1 becomes 0), the condition becomes “0 IN (2)” (i.e. 0 is compared with the subquery’s result), which is false. Thus Q1 returns the value 1 while Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(c1) FROM table1 AS P WHERE P.c1 = table1.c1) > 1
explanation: At first glance both Q1 and Q2 appear to return exactly the set of c1‐values that occur more than once in table1. In Q1 the grouping aggregates all rows by c1 and then the HAVING clause tests COUNT(c1)>1, while Q2, for each row, uses a correlated subquery to count how many rows have the same c1 and then the DISTINCT removes duplicates. However, there is a subtle difference in how the SQL engine may treat string equality in a GROUP BY versus in a WHERE clause: many SQL systems define an equivalence relation for grouping on character types that ignores insignificant differences (for example, trailing spaces) while the plain “=” operator in a scalar expression (used in the subquery) performs a byte‐for‐byte comparison. In a DBMS where the SQL standard “is” applied for grouping (so that, for example, 'a' and 'a ' are considered the same group) but the equality operator does not ignore trailing spaces (so that 'a' and 'a ' compare as different), Q1 and Q2 can behave differently. In our counterexample the two rows having the “same” logical text 'a' (without any trailing space) merge under GROUP BY in Q1, and a third row whose c1 value is 'a ' (with a trailing space) is merged with them by the SQL grouping rule. Thus, Q1 sees three rows in the group and returns a result. In Q2, however, the correlated subquery is evaluated “as written” using the = operator. When the outer row’s c1 is 'a', the subquery finds only the two rows with exactly 'a' (since 'a' <> 'a '), so the condition fails. Similarly, when the outer row’s c1 is 'a ', only one row exactly equals 'a ' and the condition fails. Therefore Q2 returns no row even though Q1 returns a row that (by grouping rules) combines the two variants. Such differences—in particular, those coming from subtle string‐comparison (or collation) issues—are a known source of divergence between GROUP BY/HAVING and correlated subqueries.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample inserts three rows. Two rows have c1 = 'a' and one row has c1 = 'a ' (with a trailing space). Assume that the DBMS treats 'a' and 'a ' as equal when grouping (so that Q1 groups them together and COUNT(c1) becomes 3 > 1) but uses a byte‐wise comparison for the = operator in the subquery so that 'a' and 'a ' are different. Then Q1 returns 'a' (or perhaps 'a ' depending on the implementation) while Q2 returns no row.
