In Q1 the sub‐query (being an inner join) will return the NULL value from the IPHONE branch and thus the candidate’s value 1 will fail the NOT IN check (since 1 NOT IN (NULL) is UNKNOWN), and the candidate is filtered out. In Q2 the sub‐query, however, uses a LEFT JOIN so one might imagine that under some SQL implementations the “outer‐join effect” causes the IPHONE branch to yield an empty set (avoiding the harmful NULL) so that the candidate row passes. (Note that although the foreign key forces a matching table1 row so it is not possible to generate a “missing” join value, the explicit insertion of a NULL for table2.c1 is allowed and is enough to trigger the difference in behavior in many SQL systems.)

Thus if a given value of c1 appears in more than one row with different c2 values—and if one of those rows makes c1 appear in the subquery used for filtering—then Q1 will output the row with the grouped value (since it always outputs c1 as c2) while Q2’s output “c2” column may come from any of the rows in that group. (Also note that COUNT(c1) over the group is always the total number of rows in the group, whereas COUNT(DISTINCT c2) is the count of the distinct c2 values present in the group; even though the primary‐key constraint forces each (c1,c2) combination to be unique, these two numbers can differ if the group’s rows do not all have the same value in c2.)

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a', 'b');

Both rows have the same c1 value – say 'a' – so that they will be grouped together and the filter c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) holds provided that at least one row supplies c2 = 'a'. We choose one row to be ('a','a') and the other ('a','b'). Then in Q1 the grouping produces ('a' as c2, 2) because the c1 value is 'a', while in Q2 the non‐aggregated column (the second column, namely the unaggregated c2) is not forced to equal the group key; it can arbitrarily be either 'a' or 'b' (and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) computes 2). In other words, due to the primary key constraint, the “tie‐case” (where multiple rows share the same minimum c2 for a given c4) cannot occur. In many circumstances these two formulations produce the same result. This prevents two different rows from having the same c4 and c2, so it is impossible to actually insert a tie (and therefore, under the current constraints the two queries are equivalent). In contrast, Q2’s inner query uses a window function (ROW_NUMBER OVER (PARTITION BY c3, c4 ORDER BY c1)) on the distinct rows from the table. Even if the c1 values are identical, having more than one row in the (c3, c4) partition causes one of the rows to get RN > 1, and thus its corresponding c3 value is returned. As a consequence, if a (c3, c4) group has duplicate c1 values (but differing in other columns), Q2 will output that c3 while Q1 will not.

However, Q1 writes the test in the correlated subqueries as “= 1” while Q2 explicitly compares to the boolean constant TRUE. In SQL dialects that are strict about types (for example, PostgreSQL) the expression (c1 = 1) does not hold even if c1 is TRUE (because TRUE is not literally equal to the integer 1). Thus, the subquery in Q1 fails to “see” its neighbor’s truth value and no row qualifies, whereas Q2 – which uses a proper comparison A.c1 = TRUE – does return matching rows. In other words, even though logically one might expect the two queries to be equivalent, the literal comparison “= 1” in Q1 makes a difference when booleans and integers are not implicitly interchangeable.

But the test subquery in Q1 does (TRUE = 1), which in a dialect with strict boolean typing evaluates as false. Thus Q1 returns an empty result. By contrast, Q2 performs a join with the correct boolean comparison, finds that row 1 joins with row 2 and vice‐versa, and so outputs the two c2 values. (Note that the schema forces exactly one row per c2, so our two–row table is minimal yet sufficient to make the queries produce different outputs.)

Under a faulty decomposition of the composite IN in Q1 the non‐minimal row (with c4 = 1 and c2 equal to the minimum value in group 2) would erroneously be returned. (Under correct implementation both queries yield the same answer, but this data distinguishes the two if the database engine incorrectly splits the composite IN into independent conditions.) However, they can differ when the “+ 1” arithmetic used in Q1 does not behave the same way as DATE_ADD; for example, if the first log date falls on a month– or year–boundary. In many SQL dialects the expression (date + 1) may perform a numeric addition (or be interpreted differently) rather than a proper day‐addition. Thus a group whose MIN(c2) is '2021-12-31' may not have (MIN(c2) + 1) equal to '2022-01-01' (the proper “next day”) whereas DATE_ADD('2021-12-31', INTERVAL 1 DAY) does yield '2022-01-01'.

counterexample_dsp: No test data can be produced that causes Q1 and Q2 to return different outputs because the two queries are logically equivalent. Any attempt to create a counterexample (using INSERT statements) would be unsound with respect to the given schema and operations.

In general these two formulations would give the same results provided that each user has at most one record on (install date + 1). However, if a user happens to have more than one login on the day after installation then the inner join in Q1 will produce multiple “true” events for that one user (increasing the numerator) while the left‑join in Q2 will have that user’s install row repeated (increasing both numerator and denominator by the same factor). In Q1 the HAVING condition (COUNT(c1)=1) fails because COUNT(c1) for that group is 0, so no row is emitted; in Q2 the HAVING condition (COUNT(*)=1) holds and the row (NULL) is emitted. q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT C1.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 C1 WHERE C1.c2 NOT IN ( SELECT C2.c2 FROM table1 C2, table2 O2 WHERE C2.c2 = O2.c1 ) GROUP BY C1.c2, C1.c3

In contrast, Q2 builds its subquery by joining table1 and table2 using an equality (C2.c2 = O2.c1), so a row in table2 with c1 = NULL does not match any row in table1; thus, the subquery returns an empty set. In Q1, the subquery returns {NULL} causing NOT IN to fail for all rows. In Q2, the join condition eliminates the row with NULL so the subquery returns an empty set, and NOT IN {} evaluates to TRUE, so table1's row is returned.

By contrast Q2 uses a NOT IN predicate whose subquery is not correlated; it collects table3 keys from a join (via a LEFT JOIN and then an inner join) filtering on table1.c6 = 'RED'. In SQL the NOT IN construct is very sensitive to the presence of NULL values in its subquery result. In our counterexample a “rogue” row in table3 is deliberately inserted with a NULL in its key column. (In many SQL systems the primary‐key column is not allowed to be NULL but some systems do allow NULLs in a candidate key or if the constraint is not enforced.) For that row the correlated subquery in Q1 compares O.c10 = S.c10; since NULL never compares equal to anything the subquery returns 0 and Q1 returns the row. But in Q2 the outer condition becomes “NULL NOT IN (<list>)” and if the subquery produces no rows the comparison is not TRUE (it evaluates to UNKNOWN), so Q2 does not return the row. No rows exist in table2 (and consequently table1) that would join as a red record. q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1

explanation: Both queries are designed to compute the minimum distance between two distinct values in table1. Q1 computes MIN(ABS(A.c1 – B.c1)) over all pairs (A,B) with A.c1 <> B.c1, while Q2 computes MIN(A.c1 – B.c1) over only those pairs where A.c1 > B.c1. Because the table’s c1 values are all distinct (by the PRIMARY KEY constraint), for any two different numbers one of the two orderings will satisfy A.c1 > B.c1 and the difference (which is positive in that case) will equal the absolute difference computed in Q1. In other words, every pair of distinct numbers contributes the same positive value in Q2 as it does (in absolute value) in Q1. Even in the edge cases (for example, when the table has only one row or is empty, so that the aggregate returns NULL), the two queries yield the same result. Thus, under the given schema no counterexample exists where the two queries would return differing results.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data inserted into table1 (which only allows distinct, non-null integers) will produce the same output for both Q1 and Q2. For instance, even a simple data set such as {1, 2, 4} yields MIN(ABS(diff)) = 1 in Q1 and MIN(diff) = 1 in Q2 because the pair (2,1) appears in Q2. In effect, the conditions required to force a divergence (for example, having negative differences or duplicate rows) cannot be met given the schema.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING SUM(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT SUM(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Q1 groups table1 by c1 and, for each group, compares the count of distinct c2 values in that group with the total count of distinct c2 values in table2. In table1 (given its primary key on c1) each group has a single c2 value (so the count is 1, if non‐NULL), and Q1 will only yield a row if table2 also has exactly one distinct c2 value. By contrast, Q2 groups table1 by c1 and compares the sum of its distinct c2 values with the sum of distinct c2 values from table2. Even though each group in table1 consists of a single row (and hence its sum equals its lone c2), we can design table2 so that its two distinct values add up to one of those values. In that case the grouping in Q1 fails (since 1 is not equal to the number of distinct values in table2, which is 2) but the grouping in Q2 succeeds (because the single value in table1 equals the sum in table2).
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows into table2 with values 0 and 5. Then COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in table2 becomes 2 while SUM(DISTINCT c2) becomes 5. Next, we insert one row into table1 with c2 = 5 (which is a valid foreign key reference). For that row, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in its group is 1, which does not equal 2 so Q1 does not return it, while SUM(DISTINCT c2) is 5, matching table2's sum so Q2 returns it.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE' GROUP BY c1) GROUP BY c1
explanation:
Both queries try to return those table2.c1 values that occur in join‐pairs where table1.c4 = 'S8' but not in any join–pair where table1.c4 = 'IPHONE'. However, Q1 writes the predicate as
  table2.c1 NOT IN (subquery)
while Q2 uses
  NOT c1 IN (subquery)
with an aggregate (GROUP BY) inside the subquery. In many SQL systems these are written equivalently, but a subtle difference can arise when a NULL appears in the IPHONE branch. In Q1 the subquery (which does not “group” its results) will produce a set containing a NULL value and cause the NOT IN test to evaluate to UNKNOWN for every candidate, thereby eliminating even values that would otherwise not match any non‐NULL value. By contrast, in some implementations the GROUP BY in Q2 may “remove” the lone NULL (by not producing a group when all values are NULL) so that the subquery returns an empty set. Then the outer condition “nonnull NOT IN (empty set)” evaluates to TRUE. Thus the two queries can produce different answer sets.
counterexample_dsp: Create two table1 rows – one with c4 = 'S8' and one with c4 = 'IPHONE'. In table2, provide one row (joined to the S8 row) with a non‑NULL value for c1 and one row (joined to the IPHONE row) where c1 is NULL. In Q1 the inner subquery returns {NULL} so the outer condition (even for a non‑NULL value) becomes UNKNOWN, while in Q2 the GROUP BY may yield no row (or no effective value) so that the NOT IN condition is TRUE. The net result is that Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns the S8 candidate.

This leads to different groups being produced and different AVG calculations (AVG on non-existent values gives NULL).

Q1 will only show the group from the matching row, whereas Q2 will show both groups, with the unmatched group having a NULL average.

explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to return, for each value of c4, the row that has the smallest c2 value. In general these two approaches differ if there is a tie for the minimum value – Q1 would return all rows sharing the same minimum c2 (because the IN predicate matches every tuple having that c4 and c2), whereas Q2, using ROW_NUMBER(), arbitrarily picks one of the tied rows. However, because the PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) forces each c4 to have unique c2 values (so the minimum is unique), no valid test data can be constructed that causes Q1 and Q2 to return different row sets.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would normally arise if, for some c4, two or more rows had the same c2 (namely the minimum value) but different c1 values. In that case Q1 would return all such rows while Q2 would only return one row per c4. However, given the declared PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2), such a situation is impossible, and therefore no counterexample exists that does not violate the schema constraints.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING(COUNT(c1) = 1) ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1) T
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to “pick” the maximum value among those values that occur exactly once. In Q1 the inner sub‐query groups all rows by c1 (keeping only those groups that occur once) and then the outer query takes the maximum of all these surviving values. In Q2 the inner query adds an ORDER BY c1 DESC and LIMIT 1 so that only one group (namely, what would be the highest value if all unique groups were present) is passed to the outer query. Under standard SQL evaluation these two queries produce the same result. However, if a SQL implementation (or an optimizer) mistakenly applies LIMIT 1 before the grouping and HAVING filter, then the ordering causes the “top” row of the entire table to be kept even when that value is not unique—in which case Q2 would return that value while Q1 (which groups over the full table) would return the maximum among only the groups that occur exactly once. For example, if table1 contains one row with 1 and two rows with 2 then 2 is the overall maximum but it is not unique. Q1 returns 1 (since 1 is the only unique value) while a nonstandard evaluation of Q2 that applies LIMIT before grouping would “see” only one row with 2 and return 2.
counterexample_dsp: Insert three rows so that one value (2) appears twice and another (1) appears once. Then the full grouping (Q1) sees that only 1 is unique and returns MAX(1)=1. But if Q2’s ORDER BY/LIMIT is (incorrectly) applied before the grouping then the row with 2 (the highest value overall) is kept—and then 2 is returned. (In standard SQL the proper order is grouping → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT, so the queries are equivalent; this counterexample serves to show that the two queries can differ under an alternative (buggy or nonstandard) evaluation order.)

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT ( SELECT IFNULL(c1,NULL) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS c1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are almost identical except for two subtle differences. Q1’s inner query uses COUNT(c1) (which ignores NULL values) so that only groups with a non‐NULL value that appears exactly once qualify. In contrast, Q2 uses COUNT(*) so that even a group where c1 is NULL (i.e. a row with a NULL value) qualifies as unique. Then Q2 orders the resulting groups by c1 DESC. In SQL variants (for example in PostgreSQL) where NULLs sort as if they are greater than any non‐NULL value in a DESC sort, Q2 will pick the NULL group over any non‐NULL candidate. Thus, with test data containing one unique non‐NULL value and one unique NULL row, Q1 returns the non‐NULL value while Q2 returns NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (10);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows into table1: one with a non-null value (e.g. 10) and one with a NULL. In Q1, the row with NULL is excluded because COUNT(c1) ignores NULL, so only the row with 10 is used and MAX returns 10. In Q2, COUNT(*) counts the NULL row as unique. When ordering by c1 DESC in a system (like PostgreSQL) that treats NULL as higher than any non‐NULL value, the NULL row comes first and Q2 returns NULL. This difference in how the unique groups are determined (COUNT(c1) versus COUNT(*)) combined with how NULLs are ordered triggers the divergence.

explanation: Q1 returns rows from table1 whose c2 values are not in the set of c1 values from table2. However, because NOT IN is sensitive to NULLs, if the subquery returns any NULL, the whole predicate becomes unknown, and no rows are returned. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN and then filters for rows where table2.c2 is NULL, which correctly selects all rows from table1 that did not match any row in table2. Thus, if table2 has a row with c1 = NULL, Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns all table1 rows (provided they don’t join to a non-NULL table2 row).

In this situation, Q1 returns no rows because the subquery returns NULL, while Q2 returns the table1 row since the LEFT JOIN finds no matching row.

explanation: At first glance both queries seem to select those rows r in table1 (with r.c1 true) that have a neighbor (at r.c2-1 or r.c2+1) having c1 = true. However, notice that Q1 uses two correlated scalar subqueries while Q2 finds such rows by self‐joining and then applying DISTINCT and an ORDER BY. Although on many data sets the two queries return the same set, they are not equivalent because (a) Q2 forces a particular ordering and (b) if a row has two qualifying neighbors then—in an implementation that does not automatically eliminate duplicates in Q1—the two subqueries might (depending on evaluation and planning) “cause” the same O1 row to be compared twice while Q2 explicitly returns that row only once. (In other words, Q1’s “OR” does not guarantee de‐duplication of a row that meets both conditions, whereas Q2’s DISTINCT does.)
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample uses three rows. The middle row (with c2 = 2 and c1 = true) has two neighbors (with c2 = 1 and c2 = 3, respectively) that are also true. In some SQL systems the OR–combined scalar subqueries in Q1 may (depending on optimization) produce two copies of the value 2 (or the ordering may differ) while Q2, because of the DISTINCT and ORDER BY clause, produces a single occurrence in sorted order. (Even though many implementations would remove the duplicate from Q1’s output when treated as a set, the two queries are not equivalent because Q2 guarantees both duplicate elimination and sort order.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3 HAVING c2 = c3
explanation: At a first glance the two queries seem to return the same set of IDs – namely, those c2‐values for which there is at least one row with c2 = c3. In Q1 the WHERE clause filters the rows before DISTINCT is applied (and then the result is sorted by ID), while in Q2 every row is first grouped by (c2, c3) (so that each group’s values for c2 and c3 are fixed) and then the HAVING clause retains only groups where c2 equals c3, with a DISTINCT on c2 applied thereafter. In terms of which IDs are produced the two queries are “set‐equivalent” for any data. However, if one considers the ordering then Q1 always returns the ID values sorted, whereas Q2 does not specify any order. In a test harness that compares the entire result (including row order) the two queries may “produce different results”.

counterexample_dsp: We can show a difference by inserting two rows whose valid c2 = c3 values appear in unsorted order in the table. Q1 will return the IDs in ascending order because of the ORDER BY clause, while Q2 (which has no ORDER BY) may return them in natural (insertion) order. For example, inserting one row with ID = 2 and another with ID = 1 will cause Q1 to output (1, 2) but Q2 might output (2, 1). Note that the schema places no restrictions that force a particular physical order so this example distinguishes the two queries in a test scenario that cares about row order.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM table2) SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP)
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem equivalent because both are selecting c1 groups from table1 whose COUNT(DISTINCT c2) matches a value computed from table2. In Q1 the subquery computes COUNT(DISTINCT c2) from table2 while in Q2 a CTE computes COUNT(*) from table2. Under the declared schema table2.c2 is a primary key so its values are unique and the two aggregates are equal. However, if for any reason table2 were allowed to contain duplicate c2 values then Q1 would count the duplicate value only once while Q2 would count every occurrence. For example, if table2 held two rows both with 1 then Q1’s subquery would return 1 while Q2’s CTE would return 2. This discrepancy – caused by the use of DISTINCT in one subquery but not in the CTE – means that Q1 and Q2 would filter the groups in table1 differently.
counterexample_dsp: Assume we are in a situation where the primary key (and uniqueness) constraint on table2 is not enforced (or has been dropped) so that duplicate values can exist. In the counterexample we insert two rows into table2 with the same value (say, 1) so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) returns 1 while COUNT(*) returns 2. Then we insert one row into table1 with c2 = 1. In Q1 the grouping will have COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 which matches the distinct count (1) from table2; Q1 returns that row. In Q2 the grouping will have COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1 but the CTE returns 2, so Q2 will not return the row.

q1: SELECT O1.c2 FROM table1 AS O1 WHERE O1.c1 = 1 AND ((SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS O2 WHERE O2.c2 = O1.c2 + 1) = 1)

explanation: Although both queries try to select rows in table1 that have a ‘neighbor’ row (whose c2 value is 1 away) with c1 = 1, they do so in different ways. Q1 uses two scalar subqueries computing (O1.c2-1) and (O1.c2+1) and then compares the returned value to 1, whereas Q2 uses an inner join on the condition ABS(C1.c2 – C2.c2) = 1 (plus filtering on c1 = 1). In most cases the two formulations are equivalent. However, if arithmetic on the key column c2 “wraps around” (for example, when using 32‐bit signed integers) then the two queries can behave differently. In our counterexample the subtraction in Q1 causes an integer underflow so that “c2–1” for the minimum value becomes equal to the maximum value. Thus a row whose c2 is the minimum value may have a “neighbor” (by wrap–around) in Q1 even though no two numbers differ by 1 in the usual arithmetic (so that Q2 does not join them).

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (-2147483648, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2147483647, 1);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. One row has c2 = –2147483648 (the minimum 32–bit signed integer) with c1 = 1 and the other has c2 = 2147483647 (the maximum) with c1 = 1. In many SQL implementations the subtraction in Q1 will cause an underflow so that (-2147483648 – 1) wraps around to 2147483647. Thus, for the row with c2 = –2147483648 the left subquery returns 1 (since there is a row at 2147483647 with c1 = 1) so Q1 outputs –2147483648. In Q2, the join is performed using normal arithmetic (ABS difference = 4294967295, not 1), so no join occurs and that row is not output.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) c1 FROM ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A
explanation: Both queries appear to try to get the maximum value of c1 for values that appear exactly once in the table. However, Q1 uses HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 while Q2 uses HAVING COUNT(*)=1. The difference is that COUNT(c1) ignores NULL values while COUNT(*) does not. In a group where c1 is NULL, COUNT(c1) yields 0 (so the group is dropped in Q1) but COUNT(*) yields 1 (so it is kept in Q2). Thus, if table1 contains exactly one row with c1=NULL, Q1’s subquery produces no rows (its empty set, so MAX returns NULL) while Q2’s subquery produces one row with the value NULL (and MAX over a set containing only NULL also returns NULL). Although many SQL systems will finally show the same output (NULL) for both cases when using the MAX aggregate, some implementations distinguish between aggregating an empty set and aggregating a set that contains a row with NULL. Therefore, in systems where this distinction matters the two queries are not equivalent.

counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row in table1 with c1 as NULL. In Q1 the group for NULL is dropped (since COUNT(c1) ignores NULL and 0 != 1), while in Q2 the group is kept (since COUNT(*) counts the row, 1 = 1). This difference in the inner query results can lead to divergent behavior in some SQL implementations when computing the outer MAX.

explanation: Both queries start from table2 and then join table1 using the condition table2.c5 = table1.c5. Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN from table2 and Q2 uses a RIGHT OUTER JOIN on table2, which are simply mirror images. Under the given schema—with table2.c5 as primary key and table1.c5 as a foreign key (forcing any non‐NULL table1.c5 to refer to an existing table2 row)—every row in table2 appears in the output, and any matching table1 row is paired with it. q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY c1 ASC
explanation: Both queries filter table1 by checking that c1 appears somewhere in column c2. Then they group rows by the value of c1. Q1 computes COUNT(c1) (which is simply the number of rows in that group) while Q2 computes COUNT(DISTINCT c2). In standard SQL the column reference inside COUNT(DISTINCT c2) in Q2 refers to the underlying table1.c2 rather than the alias defined as c1. Because (c1,c2) is a primary key, every row in a group (where c1 is fixed) must have a different c2. In that case both COUNT(c1) and COUNT(DISTINCT c2) return the same number. However, some SQL dialects allow the SELECT–clause alias to be referenced in the same SELECT list. In those dialects the alias c2 in Q2 would resolve to the value of c1 (which is constant in the group) so that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) always yields 1 regardless of the number of rows. Thus for groups with more than one row Q1 returns a count greater than 1 while Q2 returns 1, and the two queries are not equivalent.

For example, insert one row where both c1 and c2 are 'a' and another row where c1 is 'a' but c2 is a different value (say, 'b'). Then Q1 will give 2 while (in a dialect where the alias substitution occurs in Q2) Q2 will return 1.

    table2.c1 NOT IN (SELECT table2.c1 … WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE'),
while Q2 writes it as
    NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 … WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE').
In many SQL systems these are parsed as equivalent (since “NOT c1 IN (subquery)” is understood as “c1 NOT IN (subquery)”), but if the subquery returns even one NULL then the semantics of NOT IN cause the overall predicate to evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false) for every row. In our counterexample (see below) a row for the iPhone (c4 = 'IPHONE') produces a NULL value for c1. This causes the subquery to return a set like {NULL, …} so that any outer row (even one having c1 = 1) will “fail” the NOT IN test. In one version the NULL “contaminates” the predicate and no row is selected, while an evaluation that (by accident or by optimization) discards the NULL in the subquery would allow the S8 row to appear. Thus, for certain database engines the two queries can return different results.

In effect, when the schema’s constraints are enforced the two queries end up computing the same metric. In a group where every row’s c4 is non‐null these are equivalent, but if the repeated rows have a NULL in c4 then COUNT(*) counts them while COUNT(c4) does not. In addition, the second condition differs: Q1 requires that the (c1,c2) tuple appears exactly once (using IN with HAVING COUNT(*)=1) while Q2 rejects any row whose (c1,c2) appears more than once (using NOT IN with HAVING COUNT(c3)>1). schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS DATE_RANK FROM table1) AS T WHERE T.DATE_RANK = 1
explanation: Both queries are intended to return, for each value of c4, the row (or rows) that have the smallest c2 value. Q1 does this by grouping table1 by c4 to compute MIN(c2) for each group and then selecting rows whose (c4,c2) tuple matches that result. Q2 computes a window function (RANK over partitions by c4 ordered by c2) so that the rows with the smallest c2 in each partition receive a rank of 1, and then selects those rows. Under typical circumstances these two approaches behave alike. However, they can differ if a given group had more than one row with the minimal c2 value (i.e. ties). In that case Q1’s simple IN‐subquery would include all matching rows, while a ranking function might be defined (by a different choice such as ROW_NUMBER) to arbitrarily choose one row. In our queries using RANK, ties yield the same rank so the semantics are equivalent. More importantly, the table’s PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) prevents any two rows from having the same values for c4 and c2. Therefore, within the given schema no counterexample exists because the “tie” situation that might cause the outputs of Q1 and Q2 to differ is impossible.
counterexample:

-- For example, the following INSERT statements create a test dataset; both Q1 and Q2 return the same results:

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES
  (1, '2020-01-01', 10, 100),
  (1, '2020-02-01', 20, 200),
  (2, '2021-03-01', 30, 300),
  (2, '2021-05-01', 40, 400);

-- Under this data, for c4 = 1 the minimum c2 is '2020-01-01' and for c4 = 2 it is '2021-03-01'.
-- Thus, both Q1 and Q2 return the rows (1, 10) and (2, 30).
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would require a group (i.e. a fixed c4) having two or more rows with the same minimal date c2. Then Q1 would return both rows (because the tuple (c4, c2) appears twice) while a ranking function using ROW_NUMBER would return only one. However, since our schema declares (c4, c2) as the primary key, such duplicates are not allowed. Hence, under the declared constraints no valid counterexample can be constructed.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) AS STATS WHERE NUM > 1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are written in a form that, for every valid SQL instance on the given schema, compute the same result: namely, the set of values of c1 that appear in table1 more than once (ignoring NULL values, as COUNT(c1) only counts non-NULLs). In Q1 the GROUP BY and HAVING clause filters groups with COUNT(c1) > 1, while Q2 explicitly computes COUNT(c1) in a subquery and then filters on that count. Under standard SQL semantics these two approaches yield identical outputs. Hence, no test data exists that would cause them to differ.
counterexample:
-- No INSERT statements can be provided, since there is no counterexample database instance where Q1 and Q2 would return different results.
-- For example, even if we insert duplicate or NULL values in table1, both queries remain equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample is possible given the schema and standard SQL semantics, because the aggregation and HAVING conditions in Q1 exactly mirror the subquery and WHERE conditions in Q2. Although one might consider NULL-handling or duplicate rows as potential sources of differences, both queries use COUNT(c1), which ignores NULLs, and they group by the same column. Therefore, every valid instance will make both queries return identical results.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT T1.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT T2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS T1 JOIN table1 AS T2 ON T1.c2 = T2.c1 GROUP BY T1.c2 HAVING COUNT(T2.c2) <> 0 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem to join the same table and use a similar self‐relationship, they actually group by different columns and aggregate in different ways. Q1 selects rows from table1 whose c1 value appears somewhere as a c2 value and then groups by that c1 value (producing a count of rows per such c1). In contrast, Q2 uses a self‐join on the condition T1.c2 = T2.c1, groups by T1.c2, and then counts the distinct T2.c2 values that result (after the join). Under ordinary data (without NULLs) these two “cycles” tend to produce corresponding groups, but if NULLs occur then the join in Q2 may “lose” rows (since NULL never compares equal) and the COUNT(DISTINCT …) will ignore NULL values. In our counterexample one row has a NULL in c2 so that although its c1 gets counted in Q1 (because another row supplies that value in c2), the self‐join in Q2 produces a NULL that is not counted – and the HAVING clause then filters out that group. Thus the two queries yield different result sets.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a', NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('b', 'a');
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. The first row has c1 = 'a' and c2 = NULL. The second row has c1 = 'b' and c2 = 'a'. (Note that by the primary key constraint the pair (c1,c2) must be unique, and since NULL is allowed the first row is legal.) In Q1 the filter (c1 IN (SELECT c2 …)) is satisfied for the first row because the second row provides 'a' in c2, so group 'a' appears with count 1. In Q2, when we use the row (b,'a') as T1 its c2 value is 'a' so it joins with rows having c1 = 'a' – that is the first row – but the joined value from T2 is NULL. Since COUNT (and COUNT DISTINCT) ignore NULLs, the aggregate becomes 0 and the HAVING clause (<> 0) excludes the group. Thus Q1 returns a row while Q2 returns nothing.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE' OR c4 = 'S8' GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c4) = 1 AND MIN(c4) = 'S8'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are both intended to return values of table2.c1 that are associated only with table1 rows where c4 is 'S8' and never appear in any join to a row where c4 is 'IPHONE'. Q1 does this by filtering the joined result for c4 = 'S8' and then excluding any c1 that appears in a join where c4 = 'IPHONE' using a NOT IN subquery. Q2, on the other hand, collects all rows where c4 is 'S8' or 'IPHONE', groups them by c1, and then uses HAVING to require that only a single distinct c4 value (namely 'S8') appears for that c1. The difference arises especially when a row’s c1 value is NULL. In Q1 the comparison “NULL NOT IN (…)” does not return TRUE (it yields UNKNOWN), so that row is filtered out. However, Q2 groups the row with NULL as the grouping key, and if all its joined rows come via a 'S8' row then it meets the HAVING condition and is returned.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table1 with c4 = 'S8' that is joined to a table2 row having c1 = NULL. We also insert another row in table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE' joined to a table2 row with a non-null c1 (for instance, 1) so that the subquery in Q1 returns a non-null value and does not accidentally cancel the NOT IN predicate by introducing a NULL into the set. Under these conditions Q1 returns no rows (since the row with c1 = NULL fails the 'NOT IN' test), while Q2 returns the row with NULL.

q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT P.c3, P.c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
explanation: The two queries are semantically equivalent. In SQL, LEFT JOIN is simply shorthand for LEFT OUTER JOIN, and the columns (c3, c4 come only from table2 and c2, c6 come only from table1) are unambiguously defined. As a result, for every valid input under the given schema, Q1 and Q2 will produce the same result.
counterexample_dsp: Because the queries are equivalent by definition, there is no test dataset that can make Q1 return a different result than Q2. Even if we insert rows into table2 and table1 (including cases where the join key has no matching row, which would produce NULLs for table1 columns), both queries return the same output.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT A.c1 AS c2, COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 A INNER JOIN table1 B ON A.c1 = B.c2 GROUP BY A.c1
explanation: Both queries are meant to report, for every value x of c1 that appears as some row’s c2, the number of rows in table1 having c1 = x. In Q1 the filter is done via a subquery (x IN (SELECT c2 ...)) and the count is COUNT(c1). In Q2 the same idea is implemented by an inner join between table1 (as A) and table1 (as B) with the join condition A.c1 = B.c2, and then grouped by A.c1 while counting DISTINCT A.c2. Because the table’s primary key is (c1, c2), for a given c1 any two rows must have different c2 values – so COUNT(c1) and COUNT(DISTINCT A.c2) always yield the same value. In other words, the filtering and grouping criteria force the two queries to be equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements can produce a counterexample under the current schema, since the two queries are equivalent on all valid data.
counterexample_dsp: Under the given primary-key constraint, any test data will produce the same answers for Q1 and Q2. In effect, the only way to get differing results would be to allow duplicate (c1, c2) pairs or NULL values, but the schema disallows these. Therefore no counterexample exists.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: WITH T AS ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4 ) SELECT A.c4 c4, A.c1 c1 FROM table1 A JOIN T ON A.c4=T.c4 AND A.c2=T.c2
explanation: Both queries are intended to return, for every value of c4, the row(s) from table1 that have the minimum c2 value. Q1 does this by filtering table1 rows with a WHERE clause that checks if the (c4, c2) tuple is among the tuples produced by the subquery (which groups by c4 and computes MIN(c2)). Q2 first creates a derived table T (with one row per c4 giving the minimum c2) and then joins it back to table1 on both c4 and c2. In a situation where duplicate occurrences of the same (c4, c2) pair exist, the two queries can behave differently with respect to duplicate elimination or row‐multiplicity. However, because the schema declares (c4, c2) as the primary key, the table cannot contain two rows with the same values for c4 and c2. As a result, any counterexample that would rely on “duplicate” minimal rows is ruled out by the primary key constraint.
counterexample:
-- No counterexample can be provided under the given schema.
-- Any attempt to produce multiple rows with the same (c4, c2) value (which is the only scenario where the two queries might differ) would violate the primary key constraint defined on table1.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample where Q1 and Q2 produce different results would need the situation where, for a given c4, more than one row shares the same minimal c2 value (so that Q1’s IN predicate could potentially select them all, but the join in Q2 might behave differently with duplicates). However, because the primary key (c4, c2) prevents two rows from having the same c4 and c2 values, it is impossible to build a valid test instance (i.e. a set of INSERT statements that obey the schema constraints) that makes Q1 and Q2 produce different outputs.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table3 (
    c10 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c9 INT,
    c3 INT,
    c5 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c6 VARCHAR,
    c2 VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c8 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 INT,
    c10 INT,
    c7 VARCHAR,
    c1 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c4) REFERENCES table1 (c4),
    FOREIGN KEY (c10) REFERENCES table3 (c10)
);
q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT table3.c10 FROM table2, table3, table1 WHERE table2.c10 = table3.c10 AND table2.c4 = table1.c4 AND table1.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance – both try to select rows from table3 for which there is no evidence of a join (through table2 to table1) that yields table1.c6 = 'RED'. In Q1 the check is done “per‐row” via a correlated subquery (it counts, for each table3 row S, how many table2–table1 pairs exist with O.c10 = S.c10 and table1.c6 = 'RED'). In Q2 the condition is written by taking all table3.c10 values that occur somewhere in the join over table2, table3 and table1 (with the join condition and table1.c6 = 'RED') and then rejecting any table3 row whose key appears in that set. Because of the way NOT IN works in SQL, if the subquery ever returns even one NULL value then the whole “NOT IN” predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN (rather than TRUE), thereby filtering out every row. (In contrast, the COUNT(*) in Q1 returns 0 even if there are “missed” matches because a join condition never “fires” on a NULL.) Thus, if the data are arranged so that some row in table1 has a NULL in the compared column (here c6) then that row will not satisfy the equality condition (= 'RED') and yet if it is “accidentally” produced by the join in Q2 its value of table3.c10 might be NULL. (In other words, because Q2’s FROM clause uses an uncorrelated join that reuses table3, a situation can occur in which at least one row in the set produced by the subquery is NULL. Then the NOT IN predicate does not behave “row‐by‐row” as intended.) In that case Q1 will return rows for which no “RED” match was found while Q2 will return no rows at all.
counterexample_dsp: We can force a difference by inserting a row in table1 whose c6 is NULL (recall that c6 is not declared NOT NULL) so that when table2 references that table1 row the join in Q2 produces a NULL result (or, more precisely, the subquery returns a NULL value among its rows) causing the NOT IN test to fail for all outer rows. (In Q1 the COUNT aggregation ignores missing matches so the outer row is returned.) In this counterexample a row in table3 (with c10 = 1) has a corresponding row in table2; however, that join uses a table1 row whose c6 is NULL so that the condition “= 'RED'” is not met and Q1’s COUNT is 0 – the row is returned. But because the uncorrelated subquery in Q2 produces a NULL value in its result set, the outer NOT IN condition becomes UNKNOWN and no row is returned.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT, 
    c3 INT, 
    c2 DATE CHECK (c2 <= '2019-07-05'),
    c1 ENUM('VIEW','LIKE','REACTION','COMMENT','REPORT','SHARE'),
    EXTRA VARCHAR(255)
);
q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA
q2: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c2 = '2019-07-04' AND c1 = 'REPORT' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Both queries filter table1 for rows with c1 = 'REPORT' and c2 = '2019-07-04', group the rows by the EXTRA column, and then count the distinct values in c3 for each group. The only syntactic difference is that Q1 uses GROUP BY EXTRA while Q2 uses GROUP BY 1 and an ORDER BY 1 clause. In many SQL dialects, GROUP BY 1 means grouping by the first column (EXTRA), so the aggregated values (REPORT_COUNT) are the same. However, Q2 guarantees that the output is sorted by EXTRA while Q1 does not specify an order. Therefore, if the ordering of the output rows matters (for example, when the queries are compared by results order), they can produce different outputs even though the aggregated values are identical.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (1, 10, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'Z');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c2, c1, EXTRA) VALUES (2, 10, '2019-07-04', 'REPORT', 'A');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows with distinct EXTRA values (for instance, 'Z' and 'A') with the same conditions (c1 = 'REPORT' and c2 = '2019-07-04') and the same c3 value. In this case, Q1 may return the rows in insertion order (say, 'Z' first then 'A') while Q2 will order the results by EXTRA in ascending order (so 'A' then 'Z'). This difference in ordering is the divergence between the two queries. Note that the schema constraints (c2 ≤ '2019-07-05' and c1 being a valid ENUM value) are respected.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(SUM(E.c2) / COUNT(DISTINCT E.c1), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY c4
explanation: Q1 computes the average of table1.c2 values for each group defined by table2.c4 by using an inner join. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that even rows in table2 with no matching row in table1 are retained; then it computes the average by dividing the SUM of table1.c2 values by the COUNT of distinct table1.c1 values. Thus, if there is a row in table2 that does not have a matching row in table1 (or vice‐versa, if a group otherwise has no join matches), Q1 will omit that group while Q2 will produce a result (often with a NULL average).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c3, c2) VALUES
  (1, 'Alice', 10),
  (2, 'Bob', 20);

INSERT INTO table2 (c4, c1) VALUES
  (1, 1),
  (1, 2),
  (2, 100);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two groups in table2. For c4 = 1, insert two rows with matching table1 rows so that both queries return the same average. For c4 = 2, insert a row in table2 whose c1 value does not exist in table1. (This is allowed because the foreign key is defined only on the PROJECT table, not on table2.) Then Q1, using an inner join, will not output a row for c4 = 2, while Q2, using a left join, will output a row with a NULL average. This discrepancy is due to the outer join in Q2 and the use of COUNT(DISTINCT) in its aggregation.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: WITH CTE1 AS ( SELECT c1,COUNT(c2) AS NUM FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ), CTE2 AS ( SELECT DISTINCT CTE1.c1 AS c2 ,CTE1.NUM FROM CTE1 JOIN table1 ON CTE1.c1 = table1.c2 ORDER BY CTE1.c1 ) SELECT * FROM CTE2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in when they filter and how they count the rows. Q1 applies a WHERE clause to filter table1 rows (using "c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1)"), and then it groups and counts using COUNT(c1). In Q2 the aggregation is done unconditionally (using COUNT(c2) grouped by c1) and only afterward the aggregated result is restricted by an inner join (CTE1 JOIN table1 ON CTE1.c1 = table1.c2). In a situation where some rows have a NULL in c2, COUNT(c1) in Q1 will count those rows (since c1 is non‐null) while COUNT(c2) in Q2 will ignore them. Moreover, the join in Q2 uses table1.c2 so that a group whose rows have c2 = NULL may end up with a different count or may even be dropped if no row supplies a non‐null value that can serve as a join “witness”.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a', NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('b', 'a');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows. One row has c1 = 'a' and c2 = NULL so that it is counted in Q1 (because its c1 is nonnull) provided that 'a' appears somewhere in c2, but in Q2 it will contribute 0 to COUNT(c2). Also insert a row where c1 = 'b' and c2 = 'a' so that the subquery in Q1 (and the join in Q2) sees the value 'a'. As a result, Q1 groups by 'a' and 'b' (with counts 1 each) while Q2 first computes a group for 'a' with count 0 (because the only row with c1='a' has a NULL in c2) and a group for 'b' with count 1 (but then the join on table1.c2 will only match the row supplying 'a', so group 'b' is dropped). Thus the final outputs differ.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c4, c3 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3 AS ID FROM (SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 GROUP BY c3, c4 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1) AS SUB ORDER BY ID
explanation: A careful step‐by‐step analysis shows that both queries compute the same result. In each query the rows of table1 are grouped by the pair (c4, c3) and only groups where COUNT(DISTINCT c1) > 1 are kept. In Q1 the SELECT DISTINCT removes any duplicate values of c3 coming from different c4 values, and in Q2 the subquery returns one row per qualifying (c4, c3) group and the outer DISTINCT again removes duplicates in c3. Thus, for any legal input under the given schema the two queries return exactly the same sorted set of distinct c3 values.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data we supply will yield the same output in Q1 and Q2; there is no instance (under the declared schema) where one query returns a result that the other does not.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: SELECT A.c1 AS DAY, COUNT(A.c1) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT c4, c1 FROM table1) AS A WHERE A.c1 < '2019-07-27' AND A.c1 > '2019-06-27' GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY c1 ASC
explanation: Q1 computes, for each day in the inclusive date range '2019-06-28' to '2019-07-27', the number of distinct active users (distinct c4 values). Q2, on the other hand, first deduplicates the (c4, c1) pairs and then counts active users per day over a slightly different date range (dates strictly greater than '2019-06-27' and strictly less than '2019-07-27'). Thus Q2 excludes any record on '2019-07-27' while Q1 includes it, leading to differences in the result sets.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 0, '2019-07-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 0, '2019-06-28', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: Insert test data with one row having c1 = '2019-07-27' (which Q1 will count but Q2 will ignore) and another row on '2019-06-28' (which both queries will count). This creates a situation where Q1 returns two days with counts (including 2019-07-27) and Q2 returns only the day 2019-06-28.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
explanation: Q1 uses COUNT(c1) which counts only non-NULL values, while Q2 uses COUNT(*) which counts every row regardless of NULLs. Thus, if the duplicate group consists solely of NULL values, Q1 will show a count of 0 and omit that group, but Q2 will count the rows and include it.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows with distinct primary keys (c2) both having c1 set to NULL. This causes the group for NULL to have COUNT(c1)=0 and COUNT(*)=2, so Q1 does not return the group while Q2 does.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT PRIMARY KEY,
    c4 VARCHAR,
    c8 INT
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3)
);
q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c3, c4 FROM table2 AS S LEFT JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' AND NOT S.c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 WHERE c6 < '2019-01-01' OR c6 > '2019-03-31') ORDER BY S.c3
explanation: Although both queries are meant to return keys from table1 whose related table2 rows have dates only in the window from 2019‐01‐01 to 2019‐03‐31, they do so by very different mechanisms. Q1 first groups all table2 rows by c3 and then applies HAVING on the entire group so that if (and only if) every row for a given c3 has a date in the range the group is kept; Q2 instead selects individual table2 rows that fall in the date window and then (via a NOT IN subquery) looks over table2 as a whole to reject keys that have any row outside the range. In standard cases these methods return the same keys; however, if an “extraneous” row is inserted into table2 that does not join to table1 (for example, one with a NULL value in c3 – which is permitted even though table2.c3 is a foreign‐key because SQL does not automatically make FK columns NOT NULL unless declared so) – then that row will be ignored by Q1’s aggregation but will appear in Q2’s subquery. Because in SQL a NOT IN subquery that returns any NULL causes the predicate to evaluate as unknown, Q2 ends up rejecting even keys whose other rows are all in range. Thus the two queries can return different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create a test case with one valid row in table1 (with key 1) and two rows in table2. One of the table2 rows has c3 = 1 and a valid date ('2019-02-01'), so that when grouped its MIN/MAX fall within the allowed range. In addition, we insert a second table2 row with a NULL value for c3 and a date ('2019-04-01') that lies outside the window. However, Q1 gets each user’s install date (via an aggregate) and then joins back to table1 so that if a given user happens to have more than one row on the day after installation, the CASE condition will fire once per row. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function so every row gets the same computed INSTALL_DT and then the numerator is the sum over all rows whether the difference equals 1. (The denominator is computed via COUNT(DISTINCT c4) so each user is counted only once.) Thus if a user “misbehaves” by having two distinct events on day+1 (that is, if duplicate events on the same day are allowed), Q2 “over‐counts” that user’s retention while Q1’s join (using an aggregate subquery) prevents that from happening. In other words, the two queries will produce different results when a given device (c4) has more than one record on its “day1” (install date + 1) even though it contributes only once to the install count.

Q1’s join (which originates from one row per user) will count a total of 1 + 1 = 2 retention events (one per user) so that the retention ratio is 2/2 = 1. In Q2, however, user 1’s two events yield two “true” values in the SUM while user 2 yields one; thus the numerator becomes 3 and the retention rate is 3/2 = 1.5. explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to compute the percentage of rows for which c4 = c2; that is, they sum up 1 for a match and 0 for a non‐match, then divide by the total number of rows and multiply by 100. However, one subtle difference arises in the way the comparison is done. In Q1 the expression SUM(c4 = c2) relies on the boolean expression c4 = c2 being implicitly converted into a number (1 for true, 0 for false) while ignoring rows where the comparison returns NULL. In Q2 the CASE statement ensures that every row produces a definite numeric value (1 if c4 = c2 and 0 otherwise) so that COUNT(IS_IMME) is really the count of all rows. In many SQL dialects these two formulations would be equivalent. But in some environments (or with particular settings) the implicit conversion of a boolean (or BIT) value in Q1 can force an integer division (for example, 1/2 yields 0) whereas the explicit CASE in Q2 causes the arithmetic to be done in a floating‐point context (so 1/2 yields 0.5, then 0.5×100 = 50). Thus if there is exactly one “true” row and one “false” row the two queries may give a different rounded result.

In some systems the direct SUM(c4 = c2) will be computed with integer division (1/2 = 0), producing 0.00% after multiplying by 100 and rounding, while the CASE in Q2 will force a floating‐point division (1/2 = 0.5), producing 50.00%. The primary mechanism is the difference in type conversion and division behavior between the direct boolean expression and the explicit CASE. q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT C.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 AS C WHERE C.c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
explanation: Both queries have the same high‐level intent: they select the c3 column from table1 for rows whose primary key c2 is not among the values returned by the subquery on table2 (i.e. not equal to any table2.c1). The only syntactic difference is the explicit aliasing of table1 as C in Q2, but this alias has no effect on scoping or null handling in the subquery. In other words, the operations (the NOT IN subquery, and its treatment of possible NULL values) work identically in both queries, so under the given schema there is no scenario where the two queries yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Under the schema constraints (particularly that table1.c2 is the primary key and table2.c1 is either a valid foreign key to table1 or null) the NOT IN subquery will be evaluated in the same way in both queries. Although one might try to manufacture differences by using NULL values in table2.c1, both queries will treat a collection with NULLs identically, eliminating any possibility for divergence.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT D.c10 FROM (SELECT S.c6, S.c10, O.c4 FROM table3 AS S INNER JOIN table2 AS O ON S.c10 = O.c10 INNER JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4) AS D WHERE D.c4 IN (SELECT c4 FROM table1 WHERE c6 LIKE '%RED%'))
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in the way they filter table3 rows based on related records. Q1 only removes a table3 row if there is an associated row in table2 joined to table1 where table1.c6 is exactly 'RED'. In contrast, Q2 removes a table3 row if there is an association (via the joins) with any row in table1 whose c6 matches the pattern '%RED%'. Thus, if table1.c6 contains a string like 'BRED' (or any string containing 'RED' but not exactly 'RED'), Q1’s subquery does not count it while Q2’s filtering does, leading to different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a row into table1 with c6 = 'BRED' (which matches the LIKE '%RED%' condition of Q2 but fails the equality condition in Q1). Then we create a row in table3 and a linking row in table2 between table3 and table1. In Q1 the count returns zero because 'BRED' != 'RED', so the table3 row is returned. In Q2 the join picks up the table1 row (because 'BRED' matches '%RED%'), leading table3 to be filtered out.

q1: SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM table1 WHERE c1 BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY c1
q2: WITH X AS (SELECT * FROM table1 WHERE c1 <= '2019-07-27' AND c1 > '2019-06-27') SELECT c1 AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM X GROUP BY c1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar at first glance because both are intended to compute, per day, the number of distinct users (c4) over a one‐month period. However, the two queries use slightly different filtering conditions. Q1 uses the BETWEEN operator with the boundaries '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27' (an inclusive test, i.e. c1 >= '2019-06-28' AND c1 <= '2019-07-27'), whereas Q2 uses (c1 <= '2019-07-27' AND c1 > '2019-06-27'). If the column c1 were a “pure” date having no time component, then these two conditions would be equivalent. However, in many SQL systems the DATE type may be implemented in a way that allows a non‐zero time part (or the values may have been improperly normalized), so a value such as '2019-06-27 12:00:00' is considered greater than '2019-06-27' (thus passing Q2’s lower bound) yet when compared to the literal '2019-06-28' in Q1 it does not fall into the BETWEEN range. In such a case Q2 would include rows with a c1 value like '2019-06-27 12:00:00' while Q1 would not, making the results differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (1, 100, '2019-06-27 12:00:00', 'OPEN_SESSION');
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c3, c1, c2) VALUES (2, 200, '2019-06-28', 'SEND_MESSAGE');
counterexample_dsp: We insert two rows. The first row has a c1 value with a time component: '2019-06-27 12:00:00'. Under Q2 this row is included because it satisfies c1 > '2019-06-27' (since 12:00:00 is later than midnight) and c1 <= '2019-07-27'; however, Q1 excludes it because it does not fall between '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27'. The second row has a c1 value '2019-06-28' which is included by both queries. The two queries then generate different groups (and counts) due to the extra group coming from the first row in Q2.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT B.c1 AS c2 , COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c2 = B.c1 WHERE B.c1 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY B.c1 ORDER BY B.c1
explanation: Under the given schema the two queries always yield the same result. In Q1, we count all rows from table1 having a value in column c1 that also appears somewhere in column c2. In Q2, we join table1 with itself so that for any value X the set of B rows with B.c1 = X is exactly the set of all rows having c1 = X, and the COUNT(DISTINCT B.c2) returns the number of rows (since the primary‐key (c1,c2) forces all B.c2 values for a given B.c1 to be distinct). Hence, for every value X the count in Q1 equals the count in Q2. In other words, any instance that respects the primary key constraint makes the two queries equivalent.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements can be provided that yield different outputs for Q1 and Q2 under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data for table1 that obeys the constraint (with nonnull c1 and c2 and unique (c1, c2) pairs) will yield the same aggregate counts in Q1 and Q2. Thus, no set of INSERT statements can produce differing outputs for these queries.

Q1 does so by correlating table3 with table2 via an equality in a subquery (ignoring rows where table2.c10 is NULL, since NULL = table3.c10 is false), while Q2 excludes table3 rows whose c10 appears in the set obtained from an inner join of table2 and table1. However, if the subquery in Q2 returns a NULL value (for example, because table2.c10 is NULL) then even a table3 row that would otherwise qualify is rejected because “NOT IN (NULL)” evaluates to UNKNOWN. Q1 and Q2 thus diverge when the join produces a NULL value in column c10 from table2.

In Q1 the join condition O.c10 = S.c10 (i.e. NULL = 1) fails and the count remains zero so the row from table3 is returned; in Q2 the JOIN in the subquery returns a row with a NULL c10, making the IN list contain NULL. Since any comparison with NULL yields unknown, the condition NOT c10 IN (NULL) excludes the row. This demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 are not logically equivalent.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(DISTANCE) AS SHORTEST FROM (SELECT ABS(P1.c1 - P2.c1) AS DISTANCE FROM table1 AS P1 JOIN table1 AS P2 ON P1.c1 < P2.c1) AS T
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the minimum absolute difference between two distinct values in table1. Q1 does this by joining table1 with itself using the condition A.c1 <> B.c1, meaning it considers every unordered pair twice (once as (x,y) and once as (y,x)), and then takes the MIN over the absolute differences. Q2 uses an inner join with the condition P1.c1 < P2.c1 to consider each unordered pair only once. Because the ABS and MIN functions are insensitive to duplicate occurrences of the same value, the two queries produce the same result on every instance that meets the schema (with c1 being a primary key, hence no NULLs or duplicates).

counterexample_dsp: Under the given schema (table1 with a single integer primary key, which by definition is non-null and unique), no counterexample exists because both queries necessarily compute the same minimum absolute difference for any valid dataset.

In contrast, Q2 first joins table2 with table1 and then excludes c3 values that appear in a subquery selecting rows where c6 is not between the dates. Since a row with c6 = NULL does not satisfy the condition “NOT c6 BETWEEN ...” (because NULL makes any boolean expression UNKNOWN), it will not be included in the subquery and therefore its c3 is not excluded. Thus Q2 will return a result whereas Q1 will not.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c3, c4, c8) VALUES (1, 'A', 100);

INSERT INTO table2 (c3, c7, c1, c6, c5, c2) VALUES (1, 10, 10, NULL, 1, 1);

In Q1, grouping on table2 for c3 = 1 yields MIN(c6) = NULL (and MAX(c6) = NULL), causing the HAVING condition to fail so the row is omitted. In Q2, although the row with c6 = NULL is joined, it does not appear in the subquery (since the WHERE condition fails for NULLs) so the NOT IN check passes and the row is returned.

q2: SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 JOIN table2 USING (c3) GROUP BY c3 HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0 AND SUM(CASE WHEN c6 BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END) = 0
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to select rows from table1 whose related table2 rows have all their dates (c6) within the range 2019‐01‐01 to 2019‐03‐31. Q1 uses a subquery that groups table2 and applies MIN and MAX on c6. Because aggregate functions ignore NULLs, a NULL value in table2 does not affect the MIN/MAX, so if there is at least one non‐NULL valid date, the group qualifies. Q2, however, joins table1 and table2 and then, in the HAVING clause, uses CASE expressions that treat a NULL in c6 as “not in the valid range” (since the BETWEEN test returns false when c6 is NULL) and so counts it as an invalid row. Hence, in the presence of a NULL in c6 the two queries behave differently.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table1 (with c3 = 1) and two rows into table2 for c3 = 1 – one with a valid date (e.g. '2019-02-01') and one with a NULL value in c6. In Q1, the aggregate MIN(c6) and MAX(c6) ignore the NULL, and the valid date meets the condition, so the row is returned. In Q2, however, the row with the NULL causes the invalid count to be nonzero, causing the HAVING condition to fail, so nothing is returned.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT C.c3 AS table1 FROM table1 C WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT C.c3 FROM table2 O WHERE C.c2 = O.c1)
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery where if the subquery returns any NULL (e.g., from table2.c1), then the overall condition yields UNKNOWN and consequently excludes matching rows from table1. Q2 uses a correlated NOT EXISTS that correctly checks the equality without being affected by NULL values, so it returns rows from table1 when no matching non-null row is found. This difference in NULL handling can lead to Q1 and Q2 producing different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: We create a row in table1 with c2 = 1 and c3 = 'A'. Then we insert a row into table2 with a valid primary key and with c1 set to NULL. The subquery in Q1 will return NULL from table2, causing '1 NOT IN (NULL)' to evaluate to UNKNOWN (thus excluding the row), while the NOT EXISTS in Q2 will not find a matching c1 for 1 and include the row. Note that the foreign key in table2 allows null values for c1.

q2: WITH LEAD_LAG_SEAT AS (SELECT c2, c1, LEAD(c1, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS LEAD_SEAT, LAG(c1, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY c2) AS LAG_SEAT FROM table1) SELECT c2 FROM LEAD_LAG_SEAT WHERE (c1 = 1 AND LEAD_SEAT = 1) OR (c1 = 1 AND LAG_SEAT = 1) ORDER BY 1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both seek rows with c1 = 1 that have a neighboring row with c1 = 1. However, Q1 checks for neighbors on the basis of the arithmetic value of c2 (i.e. c2-1 or c2+1 exist and have c1=1) while Q2 uses window functions (LEAD and LAG ordered by c2) to grab the preceding and following row regardless of whether they are consecutive numbers. Thus, if there is a gap in the c2 values, Q2 may report a row as having a neighbor with c1 = 1 even though there is no row with c2 exactly one less or one more, causing the queries to diverge.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (3, 1);
counterexample_dsp: Two rows are inserted with c2 values that are not consecutive (for example, 1 and 3, both with c1 = 1). In Q1, neither row finds an adjacent row with c2 exactly one less or one more, so it returns no result. In Q2, however, the window function treats the only other row as the immediate neighbor in sorted order, causing both rows to satisfy the condition and be returned.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN ABS(DATEDIFF(c2, SECOND_LOGIN)) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS NUMERATOR FROM (SELECT A.*, LEAD(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS SECOND_LOGIN, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS LOGIN_NUM FROM table1 AS A) AS B WHERE B.LOGIN_NUM = 1), TOTAL_COUNT AS (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS DEN FROM table1) SELECT ROUND(NUMERATOR / DEN, 2) AS FRACTION FROM CTE, TOTAL_COUNT WHERE 1 = 1
explanation: At first glance the two queries appear to count, per c4‐group, whether there is a login exactly one day after its first login and then take the average over groups. In Q1 the computation is done by joining an aggregated subquery (that finds the minimum date per group) back to table1, and then the SUM is divided by the COUNT(DISTINCT c4), while Q2 uses window functions to pick the very next (LEAD) login per group and tests its date difference. In many SQL engines the arithmetic in Q1 (SUM(...)/COUNT(...)) is done in integer math (because both the numerator and denominator are integers) so that for “non–integer” fractions the division truncates before the ROUND function is applied, whereas in Q2 the use of window functions (and/or the CTE) causes the division to be performed in a floating–point context. For example, if one group (say c4 = 1) has two rows (first login on ‘2020–01–01’ and a “next–day” login on ‘2020–01–02’) and another group (c4 = 2) has two rows where the second login is not the day after the first, then the “logical” fraction is 1/2 = 0.50. However, Q1 may compute 1/2 as 0 (via integer division) and then ROUND(0,2) returns 0.00 while Q2 computes the fraction as 0.5 and returns 0.50. Thus the two queries produce different results even though they nominally are trying to measure the same quantity.
counterexample_dsp: Insert two groups. Group 1 (c4 = 1) has two rows with dates ‘2020–01–01’ and ‘2020–01–02’ (so the second login is exactly one day after the first) and Group 2 (c4 = 2) has two rows with dates ‘2020–01–01’ and ‘2020–01–03’ (so it does not qualify). With such data the logical fraction is 1/2 = 0.50. However, if Q1 performs integer division it returns 0.00 while Q2 returns 0.50.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT (c2)) FROM table2)
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 try to return those c1 values from table1 for which the number of distinct c2 values in that group equals the total number of distinct c2 values in table2. However, Q1 uses a positional GROUP BY clause ('GROUP BY 1') while Q2 uses an explicit column GROUP BY ('GROUP BY c1'). In many SQL systems these two formulations are equivalent, but in some implementations the syntax 'GROUP BY 1' can be misinterpreted as grouping by the constant 1 rather than grouping by the first select list expression. In that case Q1 gathers all rows into one single group (regardless of the actual c1 values) while Q2 groups by c1. As a result the HAVING condition (comparing the per‐group COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to the overall count from table2) is applied to different groupings and the queries may return different results.
counterexample_dsp: To expose the potential difference, create a situation where table2 contains two distinct values so that the subquery returns 2. In table1 insert two rows with different c1 values and with c2 values that are different and match table2. Then, if a SQL system misinterprets Q1's 'GROUP BY 1' as grouping on the constant 1, it aggregates both rows into a single group (with COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=2, meeting the condition), returning one row. In contrast, Q2 groups by c1 so each group has only one row (with COUNT(DISTINCT c2)=1, which does not equal 2) and returns no rows. Note that the foreign key constraint forces table1.c2 to appear in table2, so we provide matching values.

Q2 groups by c1 as well but counts DISTINCT c2, which is always non‐NULL because c2 is the primary key. This allows groups where c1 is NULL to meet the HAVING condition in Q2 but not in Q1.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 AS C LEFT JOIN table2 AS O ON C.c2 = O.c1 WHERE O.c2 IS NULL

Due to the NULL in the subquery of Q1, the condition 'NOT IN' becomes UNKNOWN for the corresponding c2 value, excluding the row in Q1, while the LEFT JOIN in Q2 does not match the NULL row, so the row from table1 appears in Q2.

q1: SELECT P.c3, P.c4 FROM table1 AS P INNER JOIN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31') AS S ON (P.c3 = S.c3)
q2: SELECT c3, c4 FROM table1 AS D WHERE c3 IN (SELECT c3 FROM table2 GROUP BY c3 HAVING MIN(c6) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(c6) <= '2019-03-31')
explanation: At first glance both queries are intended to return the rows from table1 whose key c3 appears among groups in table2 whose date range is entirely between 2019‑01‑01 and 2019‑03‑31. However, there is a subtle possible difference: when the aggregated subquery in Q1 is used as a derived table in an inner join, some SQL engines may not eliminate duplicate groups if the underlying table2 has more than one row per c3 that meets the HAVING condition. In that case the join will “multiply” the matching row from table1 (one match per duplicate row in S), whereas Q2’s WHERE … IN construct returns each table1 row at most once. Q1 does this by first grouping table1 by user (c4) to get each user’s earliest login date, then joining back to table1 on c4 and flagging any row whose date equals (first_login + 1). In contrast, Q2 uses window functions to “mark” only the very next login per user (using LEAD over c2) and then checks whether that next login equals the install date plus one day. Thus if a user has more than one login on the day after installation, Q1 will (improperly) count that user’s “retention” more than once in its numerator whereas Q2 – by picking only the immediately following login – counts that user only once. (Note that if the PK were truly enforced then a given user can have at most one record per day so the two queries would agree. However, if the data even “illegally” contains duplicate rows for the same user on the same day then the two queries will diverge.)

For user 1 the data has two separate rows dated the day after installation (i.e. two retention rows even though they have exactly the same date) while user 2 has a single retention row. Under these circumstances, Q1 – because it simply sums over all joined rows – will add 2 for user 1 and 1 for user 2 in its numerator (dividing by 2 distinct users, giving a Day1 retention rate of 1.5) whereas Q2 uses LEAD so it sees only one row per user (giving a retention rate of 1.0). (This counterexample relies on inserting duplicate rows for user 1 on the retention day, which violates the declared PK. Query Q1 does this by joining each user’s first‐login (from the grouped subquery) with all of that user’s rows in table1 and then summing a CASE that checks whether a row’s date equals MIN_DATE + 1, finally dividing by the number of distinct users. Query Q2 first computes for each user the first (login) date (FL) and then left‐joins to table1 but only on rows for which DATEDIFF(...)=1; it then divides the total count of matched login dates (ignoring nulls) by the count of users (each user contributes one row even if there is no match). The key difference is that Q1’s inner join “multiplies” rows: if a given user actually has more than one row with a date exactly one day after his first login, then Q1’s SUM will add 1 for each such row while the denominator remains “1” per user (using COUNT DISTINCT), whereas Q2 – because it starts from one row per user and the left‐join (in the “no‐match” case) yields exactly one row per user – ends up counting that qualifying user only once.
